conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’re here today for your gastric bypass surgery, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been preparing for this for a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see from your chart you’ve struggled with weight for years and tried programs like Weight Watchers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve lost weight before, but it always comes back. I want to be healthier for my family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Your BMI is 40, which qualifies as class III obesity, and surgery can be very effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have sleep apnea and acid reflux. I hope this helps with those too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It very likely will. Many patients see improvement in both conditions after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be a big relief. I use CPAP every night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your progress closely. Right now, we’re going to get you prepped for surgery. Any questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Just a little nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. You’re in good hands. We’ll see you after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re back in your room. The surgery went very well — laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and an endoscopy. You tolerated everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I feel groggy, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on a pain pump for now — Dilaudid PCA — so you can control your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Tomorrow we’ll start with clear liquids — that’s stage one. We’ll advance slowly to make sure there’s no leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. My pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We did an upper GI study this morning with contrast, and there’s no sign of a leak or blockage. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. Can I start drinking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids — water, broth, apple juice — in small amounts. That’s stage one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I stay on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a day or two. We’ll move you to pureed foods next, then soft solids. You’ll be on stage three by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my regular medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume them, but you’ll need to crush all pills for now — your stomach is smaller and can’t handle whole tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Even my antidepressant and Abilify?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them — citalopram, Abilify, lorazepam, and your pantoprazole for reflux. We’ll make sure they’re crushed and mixed with soft food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re advancing your diet to stage three today — soft foods like mashed potatoes and scrambled eggs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’m hungry but trying to go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Small, frequent meals — about ½ cup at a time. And no straws or gum — that can cause bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. Why no straws?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can make you swallow air, which leads to bloating and discomfort. It’s best to avoid them for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re cleared to go home today. You’ve tolerated stage three diet, your incisions are dry, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the stage three diet until your follow-up. Crush all pills, take your new meds — Protonix for reflux, Actigall for your gallbladder, and Colace for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Roxicet as needed, but don’t drive or operate machinery — it can make you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have my sister help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Also, no heavy lifting over 10 pounds for six weeks. You can shower, but no baths or swimming yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if something goes wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or go to the ER if you have a fever over 101.5, severe pain, vomiting, or redness around your incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch for that. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. Follow up with Dr. Evans in two weeks. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You were admitted early this morning for epigastric pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this burning pain in my upper belly for about a day now. It’s worse after I eat. I also felt nauseous and threw up once, but it was just food—nothing strange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or changes in your bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But my stools have been looser than usual—three times today, all soft and not bloody. I’m still passing gas, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear. You had your gastric bypass surgery a few months ago and lost about 50 pounds, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about three months ago. I’ve been doing well until now. No pain or issues before this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’re going to run some tests to find out what’s causing this pain. We’ve already ordered blood work and a CT scan with contrast to look at your stomach and the bypass area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this something serious? Could it be related to the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. One possibility is an ulcer near the connection site. We’ll know more after the CT and a scope procedure later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A scope? Like an endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll pass a small camera through your mouth to look at the stomach pouch and the connection to the small intestine. It’s called an EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel much. Just some pressure. We’ll do it after the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. It shows contrast in both your gastric pouch and the remnant stomach, which suggests there might be a small connection between them—possibly a fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fistula? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s an abnormal passage between two areas that shouldn’t be connected. In your case, between parts of your stomach. It’s not common, but it can happen after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the pain and ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could contribute. We’re about to do the EGD to look more closely. We’ll also check for ulcers and take a blood test for H. pylori, a bacteria that can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re awake. The EGD is done. We found two ulcers near the connection site—on the jejunal side, about 2 cm past the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Are they bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One is 8 mm and superficial, the other is 1.5 cm and deeper, with a dark spot in the center. But there’s no active bleeding, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. The fistula is between the pouch and remnant stomach. The ulcers are downstream, near where the stomach connects to the intestine. They may be related, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes ulcers like this after bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Several things—like acid exposure, certain medications, or even smoking. But you don’t smoke, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, never smoked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also sent a blood test for H. pylori. It came back negative, so that’s not the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on a strong acid-reducing medication called Protonix, given through your IV. It helps ulcers heal. We’ll also control your pain with IV morphine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Most of these ulcers heal with medication and diet changes. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still some discomfort, but not as sharp. The morphine helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch your pain medicine to oral Roxicet and start you on a bariatric stage 2 diet—soft foods like mashed potatoes and scrambled eggs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to let the ulcers heal. You’ll stay on soft foods for now, then advance to stage 3 later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your pain is still improving, and you’ve tolerated the soft diet well. We’re going to advance you to bariatric stage 3—more solid foods, but still easy to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I’ve been having loose stools in the evenings. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the changes in your digestion after surgery. We’ll switch you to a lactose-free diet to see if that helps. Sometimes dairy can cause diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think about that. I had some yogurt yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be it. We’ll hold off on dairy for now. Also, we’re switching your Protonix from IV to oral. You’ll take it by mouth twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take that forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least for a few months. We’ll reassess at your follow-up. The goal is to let the ulcers heal completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve done really well. Pain is minimal, you’re eating well, and your labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the omeprazole twice a day—crush the pill and mix it with applesauce. Take the oxycodone only if you need it for pain. And stay on the lactose-free diet for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your pain is controlled without narcotics. I’ll give you a note. Follow up with your surgeon in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m glad it wasn’t something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Call us if the pain worsens or if you notice black stools or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking my vitamins and CPAP at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Those are important. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—avoid heavy lifting and straws. They can increase pressure on the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No straws, no heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you. The nurse will go over your medications and paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling weak and nauseous. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had nausea for about a week now and I can’t keep anything down—not even water. I felt so weak today I knew I had to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were here recently for epigastric pain and a marginal ulcer after your gastric bypass, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was on omeprazole and it was helping, but then the nausea came back and I couldn’t eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll start by giving you IV fluids to rehydrate you. We’ll also continue the proton pump inhibitor through the IV to protect your stomach lining, since you have a history of ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon? I’m really worried about not getting enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Right now, we need to control the nausea. We’re giving you ondansetron for that. Once you’re stable, we’ll try small sips and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any change in the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, I think. The pain in my stomach is less, but I still feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to add a medication called sucralfate. It coats the ulcer and helps it heal. You’ll take it four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the nausea still related to the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’re also watching for other causes. We’ll keep monitoring you and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have some news. You started having diarrhea yesterday, so we sent a stool sample. It came back positive for C. diff—Clostridium difficile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff? Is that serious? How did I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an infection that can happen after antibiotics or in hospital settings. It’s treatable. We’re starting you on metronidazole, an antibiotic that targets C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, over the next few days. We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now and monitor your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea is still ongoing, so we consulted Infectious Disease. They agree with continuing metronidazole for a full 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because I’m on the omeprazole? I heard that can increase the risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right—PPIs can increase the risk of C. diff. But we still need to protect your stomach from ulcers, so we’ll continue it with caution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your diarrhea has improved a lot since yesterday. That’s a sign the metronidazole is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can finally catch my breath. Can I try eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids and advance slowly to your stage 3 bariatric diet. Small, frequent meals—no straws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time—no straws, no gum. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Nausea is gone, and you’re tolerating solids. Your labs are stable, and you’re well-hydrated now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re heading that way. We’ll make sure you’re on the right medications and have a clear plan before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on your discharge plan. You’ll continue omeprazole twice a day, sucralfate four times a day, and metronidazole three times a day for six more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to crush all my pills, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And stick to chewable vitamins—no gummies. We’re also adjusting your vitamin D dose to 1,000 units daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re up and walking, eating well, and your symptoms are resolved. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up a follow-up with your surgeon. In the meantime, avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to acetaminophen if I need pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, no heavy lifting for six weeks. You can do light exercise, but avoid anything that strains your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy. What about my CPAP? Should I keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Continue your CPAP at night. It’s important for your breathing and overall recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your labs are normal, you’re afebrile, and you’ve had no pain or nausea. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like a new person.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over your discharge instructions one more time to make sure everything is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is your last day. You’re tolerating your stage 3 diet, walking independently, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What symptoms should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or go to the ER if you develop a fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep taking the metronidazole until it’s all gone, even after I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finish the full course. It’s important to prevent the infection from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll follow up with my surgeon in two weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll assess your progress and adjust your long-term plan if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Just take it slow at home and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions before we wrap up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I should crush all pills, stay on the stage 3 diet, and avoid NSAIDs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. And continue your vitamins and sucralfate as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel off, I should call the surgeon or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Better safe than sorry. We want you to recover fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I restart all my previous medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, except we’ve adjusted your vitamin D and omeprazole. The rest stay the same—just crush them before taking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll double-check the list you gave me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. And remember, no straws or gum—it can cause bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Just follow the plan and you’ll do fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. I’ve missed my bed!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I bet. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll start packing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call your name when it’s time to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's been going on for about five days. It's in my upper belly, both sides, and it feels different from my usual ulcer pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea, yes, but no vomiting. My stools have been darker lately, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll check for any bleeding. We’ve started IV fluids to keep you hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before after my bypass. Is it another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll need an endoscopy tomorrow to look inside. For now, we’re giving you pantoprazole through the IV to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sucralfate? I take that crushed at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that four times a day, crushed as usual. It helps coat and protect the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’m worried about the dark stools. Could I be bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. Your hematocrit was 40.5 on admission, and we’ll check it again. The dark color could be from the ulcer, but we’ll make sure it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s pretty constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you some morphine through the IV for now. We’ll reassess your pain and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also had C. diff a few months ago. Should I be tested again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve sent a stool test for C. difficile, and we’ll repeat it if needed. But so far, no diarrhea, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my CPAP? I use it every night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll bring it up from home. Sleep apnea is important to manage, especially in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from your endoscopy. The good news is we didn’t find any major bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they see?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a new small ulcer at the connection between your stomach and intestine. The large ulcer you had before is improving, and the small one from before is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re doing a CT scan today. The pain seems worse than what the endoscopy shows. We want to rule out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT show if there’s a blockage or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The CT will check for obstruction, infection, or other issues. We’ll have results later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. No blockage, no free air, which is good. But there’s a small area in your left kidney that could be a tiny infection or a small area of reduced blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A kidney infection? Could that be causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it’s small. Your urinalysis was normal, so it may not be active. We’ll watch it and repeat tests if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ulcer? What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your pantoprazole to twice a day. That helps ulcers heal faster. We’ll keep you on sucralfate too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it from H. pylori? Should I be tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a stool test. Your blood test was negative before, and the stool came back negative too. So it’s not H. pylori.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And C. diff? Was that negative too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both tests were negative. So no C. diff either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try a regular diet. Start slowly and let us know if the pain gets worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the meal go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurt for about 45 minutes after, but I was able to finish it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. Some discomfort is expected. We’re switching your pain med from IV morphine to oral Roxicet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took one earlier. It didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting us know. We’ll switch you to oral Dilaudid, which might work better for your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your pain is better with the new medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I took it last night and this morning. The pain is manageable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your hematocrit dropped a little to 38.9 but is now stable. No further blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not bleeding anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No active bleeding. The dark stools are likely from old blood. Your levels are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’d like to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel much better, but what about the kidney finding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and not causing symptoms. We’ll monitor it. No treatment needed now unless you develop fever or urinary symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times a day. Follow up with GI in six weeks for a repeat endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a small supply of Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. Use it only as needed. Avoid driving while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call my surgeon soon for a follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within the next two weeks. And call us if the pain worsens, you see black stools, or develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest, stay hydrated, and take your meds. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I avoid lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nothing over 10 pounds until you see your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team members. You're here today because you've been having a lot of trouble eating and keeping weight on due to your stomach ulcers, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve lost about 20 pounds in the last month. I feel nauseous all the time and even small meals make me uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been having constant epigastric pain, which you manage with oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps a little, but the nausea is the worst part. I can’t even keep my vitamins down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Your recent endoscopy showed persistent ulcers at the gastrojejunal anastomosis, but no bleeding. Because you're not able to eat enough, we’re going to place a tunneled central line today so you can start total parenteral nutrition—IV nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about a feeding tube. Is this different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A feeding tube goes into the stomach or intestine. Since you can’t tolerate food there, we’re bypassing the gut entirely. The central line will deliver nutrition directly into your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common procedure, especially for patients like you with malnutrition after bariatric surgery. We’ll place it under imaging guidance, and you’ll be sedated. The line will go into your jugular vein and end in your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get medication to keep you comfortable. There might be some pressure, but not sharp pain. Afterward, we’ll start you on IV fluids and begin nutrition slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll be able to go home with this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once we make sure you tolerate the nutrition. You’ll go home on a 12-hour nightly cycle. A home care team will help with line care and lab draws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was placed successfully. It’s a double-lumen catheter in your right internal jugular, tip in the right atrium. No complications. You can start receiving IV nutrition soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does it need special care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The dressing must stay clean and dry. We’ll teach you how to flush the line and recognize signs of infection—like redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if it gets wet during a shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to cover it with a waterproof shield. The home care nurse will show you how. Don’t submerge the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White count is a bit low at 3.5, but everything else looks stable. Albumin is 4.1, which is good, but your pre-albumin was low at 21, confirming malnutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the IV nutrition fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve started peripheral nutrition today and will transition to full TPN tomorrow. We’ll increase it gradually over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ulcer medicine? I’ve been on pantoprazole and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on both. We’re giving pantoprazole IV twice daily to help the ulcer heal. You’ll continue that at home by self-infusion for two months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have to give myself IV meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but don’t worry. The home care team will train you. It’s a simple push injection every 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve started your total parenteral nutrition. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is still there, but I haven’t vomited. I tried a little broth, but it didn’t stay down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll keep you on NPO for now and advance your TPN. A nutritionist will come to talk about what you might tolerate in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nutritionist said I could try a stage 1 diet later. Is that safe with the ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start very slowly—clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance step by step. But your main nutrition will come from the IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was a bit high yesterday at 163, but it’s down to 112 today. We’re adjusting the dextrose in your TPN to keep it stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had diabetes before my bypass, but it went away. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. The high glucose is likely from the TPN. We’re monitoring it closely and will taper as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pre-albumin improved from 21 to 22. It’s a small change, but it shows your nutrition is starting to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Can I try more food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a stage 3 diet today—soft, low-fat, low-acid foods. Small portions. Let us know if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate a little mashed potatoes and applesauce. No vomiting. Still nauseous, but less than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep advancing the diet. Your TPN is now at goal and cycling over 16 hours. You’re tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted the Chronic Pain team. They recommend increasing your oxycodone frequency and switching from Roxicet to plain oxycodone solution for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Roxicet wasn’t helping much. I’d like to try something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your meds. You’ll get oxycodone every 3 hours as needed, and acetaminophen for breakthrough pain. Your primary care doctor has been notified and will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to see a pain clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’d like you to follow up at the Chronic Pain Clinic. Your PCP will send a referral. Please call to schedule it when you get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’re tolerating a stage 5 diet, your vitals are stable, and your line site looks clean. We’re discharging you today on a 12-hour TPN cycle at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the ultrasound they did yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed no gallstones or liver issues. Your right upper quadrant pain isn’t from your gallbladder. We’ll keep focusing on the ulcer and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have a problem with the line at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the home care nurse for redness, swelling, or drainage. Go to the ER if the line is damaged, pulled out, or if you develop a fever over 101.5°F.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’m ready. Thank you for helping me get stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your sucralfate four times a day, crush the tablets. Continue the IV pantoprazole, and follow up with your surgeon and the pain clinic. Rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call the pain clinic as soon as I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. The home team will visit you tomorrow to check the line and review everything again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You were admitted overnight due to ongoing nausea and trouble keeping food down after your gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been so nauseous. I can’t eat more than a few bites. I’ve been relying on the TPN through my central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your history shows you had ulcers after the bypass, which are now healed, but the nausea and poor intake have continued. We’re concerned about malnutrition, which is why you’ve needed TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve lost a lot of weight. I just can’t tolerate eating. Is there anything we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The plan is to place a gastrostomy tube—what we call a G-tube—through your abdomen into your stomach. This will let us give you nutrition directly into your stomach instead of through your veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So, like a feeding tube? Will I still be able to eat by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s a feeding tube. We’ll start with tube feeds at night. Over time, you may still be able to eat small amounts by mouth, but the tube will make sure you get enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And this is done with surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a laparoscopic procedure—small incisions, camera-guided. It’s low risk, and we do it often for patients in your situation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today. The OR schedule has you set for around noon. We’ll go over consent and prep you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. You just came back from surgery. The G-tube was placed successfully—no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I didn’t feel anything—must’ve been out cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, general anesthesia. The tube is in the right spot. We’ll wait until tomorrow to start feeds, after we confirm placement with a contrast study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt when I start using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some soreness around the site, like after any small surgery. But it shouldn’t be severe. We’ll manage pain with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I’m reviewing your imaging from last night. The gastrograffin study shows the G-tube is in the correct position in your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Does that mean we can start the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition team is starting you on Fibersource HN through the tube at a low rate. We’ll increase it gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my TPN? Will I still need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already stopped the TPN. The goal is to get you fully off it. The tube feeds will replace it over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I never liked the central line. It felt like a constant reminder I wasn’t healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Once we confirm you’re doing well on tube feeds, we’ll remove the central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or discomfort from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, no. I don’t feel worse. Maybe a little full, but not sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’re keeping the rate low today, but tomorrow we’ll increase it. The goal is 80 cc per hour for 12 hours overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Overnight only? So I’m not hooked up all day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just overnight. That’s called cycled feeding. Gives your stomach a break during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re up to 80 cc/hr and tolerated it well last night. No issues with nausea or bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, actually slept better. I didn’t wake up hungry or sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s exactly what we want. We’re also going to remove your central line today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. Is it safe to remove it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, well-nourished from the feeds, and no longer need TPN. The interventional radiology team will remove it this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your central line has been successfully removed. The site is clean, no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel it. I’m so glad it’s gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the area covered for a day or two. You’re doing really well on the G-tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try eating a little by mouth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on a stage V diet—full liquids. Things like broth, yogurt, protein shakes. We’ll see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some apple juice earlier. No nausea. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. You’re off TPN, on full tube feeds, and tolerating oral intake. We’re looking at discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day—we’re getting ready to send you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel ready, but I’m a little nervous about managing the tube at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. A nurse will come to your home to help with the overnight feeds. And you’ll have detailed instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like how to check the tube before feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll use a syringe to check for residual—any leftover formula in the stomach. If it’s more than 50 ml, you’ll pause and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dressing around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wash with mild soap and water. Apply antibiotic ointment and a dry dressing until it stops draining. Once healed, you can leave it uncovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking the pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once daily. It helps prevent ulcers and protects your stomach, especially with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. Patel in two weeks. We’ll check your weight, the tube site, and how you’re doing overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I’m finally on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are. You’ve made excellent progress—off TPN, on full feeds, and tolerating food. We’re proud of how far you’ve come.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just glad I can start healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll do great. Call us if you have fever over 101.5, severe pain, or vomiting. Otherwise, rest and let the feeds do their job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge orders are in. Home health nurse will start tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send the feeding pump and supplies with you. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe this chapter is over. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Vital signs are stable—temperature normal, heart rate down from admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Abdomen is soft, no tenderness. G-tube site looks clean. You’re medically ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just need the paperwork and I’ll head out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s being printed now. Safe journey home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team members. You're here because of worsening dry heaves and trouble keeping food down. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. It started a few weeks ago—just a few dry heaves a week. But now it’s several times a day. I can’t eat much without feeling like I’m going to heave again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any vomiting with actual content, or just dry heaves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just dry heaves. No vomiting. Bowel movements are normal—no blood or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. You had a gastric bypass years ago, and then a G-tube placed, which was removed recently—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had the G-tube for nutrition, but I asked to have it removed. Since then, the pain and heaving got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your history shows you’ve had ulcers at the surgical site before. We’re concerned that might be flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the dry heaves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, irritation or an ulcer in the stomach remnant can cause nausea and retching, even without vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on IV fluids to keep you hydrated and give you a ‘banana bag’—it has vitamins and electrolytes. You’ve been on pantoprazole and sucralfate at home—we’ll continue those, but through IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve been worried about not getting enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Right now, we’re supporting you with fluids. We’re planning an upper endoscopy in the next day or two to look at your stomach pouch and the bypass connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under sedation, so you’ll be asleep. It’s very safe. We’ll use it to check for ulcers or inflammation and treat anything we see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look stable. White count is a bit low but not concerning. Your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little better today—still some nausea, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’re going to try advancing your diet today—start with a stage 4 bariatric diet. Small portions, soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Things like mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs, pureed soups. Easy to digest. We’ll watch you after the first meal to make sure you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with lunch—no heaving, and you said the food stayed down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I only had a small amount, but it felt okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep you on the IV protonix twice a day for acid suppression. The endoscopy is scheduled for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance they’ll find another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Given your history, we’re especially looking at the anastomosis and the gastric pouch. If we see an ulcer, we can treat it with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s bad, could I need another G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. Most of these can be managed with meds and diet. We’re not planning any tubes unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the endoscopy. You did great. The report shows your bypass anatomy looks good. No issues in the small intestine or connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But… there was something, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small erosion was seen in the top part of your stomach remnant—the cardia. It’s not a full ulcer, but it’s irritated and likely causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can that heal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep you on high-dose pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day. Those help protect and heal the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a stage 5 bariatric diet—regular soft foods, but still small portions. No spicy or acidic foods for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Vital signs are stable, you’re tolerating food, and your pain is controlled. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue sucralfate four times a day, pantoprazole twice daily, and metoclopramide as needed for nausea. We’re adjusting your citalopram and aripiprazole doses too—lower now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your surgeon in one week. Call us sooner if you have chest pain, vomiting, black stools, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lifting, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—nothing over 10 pounds until your follow-up. And avoid driving while on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand everything. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having nausea, stomach pain, and dry heaves for about a week and a half?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s constant pain in my upper belly, and I just can’t keep food down. I feel full after even a few bites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you’re drinking about 2 liters of water a day, but not getting enough calories. Have you noticed any vomiting blood or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no blood or dark stools. No fever either. Just this pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, that’s reassuring. Given your history of gastric bypass and previous ulcers, we want to make sure we’re not dealing with another erosion or gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had something like this before, and it was an erosion. I hope it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. For now, we’re starting you on IV fluids to rehydrate you, including a ‘banana bag’ with vitamins, since you’ve been eating so little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been feeling kind of weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also started IV pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and help any irritation heal. We’ll get some blood work to check your nutrition and organ function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. Your blood counts are a bit low, and your albumin is low too, which suggests malnutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, yes. We’ve consulted nutrition, and they agree you’re at risk. We’re going to place a PICC line so we can start TPN—total parenteral nutrition—through your vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: TPN? I’ve heard of that. It’s like IV nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It delivers calories, protein, fats, and vitamins directly into your bloodstream. We’ll start slow to avoid refeeding syndrome, then build up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully in your left arm. The chest X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot—near your heart. You should be ready for TPN soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I hope this helps me feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs today show no signs of refeeding syndrome. Your electrolytes are stable, and we’re increasing your TPN dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My nausea is still there, but maybe a little less?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you ondansetron for nausea. We’ll keep monitoring. One test came back—your H. pylori antibody test was negative, so it’s not that infection causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, so not an infection. What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be gastritis, a hiatal hernia, or even cyclic vomiting syndrome. We’ll know more after your EGD on day five.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—still no refeeding issues. TPN is at goal now. We’re starting to cycle it at night, so you’ll have freedom during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds nice. I’d like to be able to move around more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re encouraged—your nausea is improving, and pain is less intense. We’ll keep building strength for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for your EGD. It’s an upper endoscopy—we’ll look inside your stomach to see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under sedation. It’s quick, and we’ll have results by this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The EGD showed mild gastritis and a small hiatal hernia. No ulcers or bleeding. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no erosion this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. But the gastritis and hernia could explain your symptoms. Gastroenterology wants us to increase your pantoprazole to 80 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s double what I was on. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and often used for more severe reflux or hernias. We’ll switch you to IV for now, then you’ll continue at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep it for now, but we’re starting you on a stage 5 bariatric diet—small amounts of soft food—to see how you tolerate eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I’m nervous I’ll feel full too fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Eat slowly, small bites. We’re not expecting you to eat a lot yet. The TPN will cover your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Great news—you tolerated the diet well overnight, no nausea. Your pain is much better, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can actually eat again. Not much, but it’s something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. You’ll go home on TPN, cycled at night, and continue IV pantoprazole twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll still need IV meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. A nurse will visit to help with the TPN and IV meds. We’ll switch to oral meds when your stomach is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume most—like your citalopram, lamotrigine, and iron. We’ve adjusted doses. Temazepam and lorazepam are now as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see gastroenterology soon to discuss cyclic vomiting syndrome. And Dr. Patel for surgical follow-up. We’ll also need labs: liver tests, electrolytes, albumin, and triglycerides.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if my pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if pain worsens, or if you develop fever, vomiting, black stools, or trouble breathing. Also, watch for signs of dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will teach you care before discharge. Keep it clean and dry. Call if you see redness, swelling, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m glad I’m on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and we’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge paperwork is ready. You’ll receive 120 vials of IV pantoprazole for twice-daily use at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the multivitamins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold the multivitamins while on TPN—they’re included in the solution. Resume when TPN stops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use only if needed for pain, every 4 hours as needed. Don’t drive while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re also sending docusate for constipation if needed. And ondansetron for nausea—dissolve one every 8 hours if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed it today. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It really is. You’ve improved a lot in five days. Keep it up, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Your vitals are stable, you’re alert, and you’ve eaten a small meal without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared. Remember: follow-up appointments, labs, and call us if anything changes. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and keep building your strength. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The nurse will assist you with discharge now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team members. You're here today for your scheduled gastrostomy tube placement, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been having so much nausea and trouble keeping food down. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This tube will help transition you from TPN to tube feedings, which should be easier on your system. The procedure is done by interventional radiology, and you’ll be back here afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel anything during the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be drowsy and comfortable. Your vital signs will be closely watched the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. And the tube goes into my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, into the gastric remnant—your stomach pouch from the bypass. It’s placed under fluoroscopy, so they can see exactly where it goes. It’s a minimally invasive procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll start feeds right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. We’ll start with clear liquids by mouth tomorrow to make sure you tolerate that. Then, after 24 hours, we’ll begin tube feeds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my PICC line—will that stay in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove it once you’re tolerating tube feeds well. Since you’re on TPN now, we’ll keep it until we’re sure the tube feeding is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been on TPN for a while, but it’s not ideal long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The goal is to get you off TPN and onto enteral nutrition, which is safer and more natural for your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back! The procedure went smoothly. The tube is in place, and the chest X-ray confirms it’s positioned correctly in your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does it hurt? I feel a little pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some mild tenderness is normal. We’ll give you pain meds if needed. The site is dressed and secured with sutures. We’ll keep an eye on it for any signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC is still in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still in. We’ll continue your TPN and IV pantoprazole for now. Tomorrow, we’ll start you on clear liquids by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little sore, but not bad. I had some water last night and kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll start advancing your diet today. First, clear liquids, then if you do well, we’ll begin tube feeds this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of formula will I get through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting with ‘Replete with Fiber’—it’s balanced and includes fiber to help with bowel regularity. It’ll run at 110 mL per hour for 12 hours overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll still take my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds—aripiprazole, citalopram, lamotrigine, lorazepam, nortriptyline, temazepam, and pantoprazole. We’ll switch pantoprazole to oral today since you can swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feeds now. We’ll begin slowly and monitor for any nausea or bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I feel anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel a little fullness, but not pain. Let us know if you feel nauseous or crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—no nausea, and the feeds are going at goal rate. We’re going to try advancing you to a regular diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I haven’t eaten solid food in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small amounts. If you tolerate it, you can eat more. Your nausea has improved, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had a good night—feeds completed, no issues. We removed the PICC line this morning since you’re stable on enteral nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I was worried about infections from the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now we focus on your recovery at home. You’ll continue the tube feeds overnight and take pantoprazole daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain med?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxycodone-acetaminophen as needed. But use it sparingly—your pain is mild, and we want you off opioids quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see surgery in two weeks. Also, continue with gastroenterology—they’re managing your cyclic vomiting syndrome with nortriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube care at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the site clean and dry. Wash with soapy water daily. Watch for redness, swelling, or discharge. Call if you have fever or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but keep the site dry—use a waterproof cover. No baths or swimming for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You’re doing great—tolerating feeds, walking, and pain controlled. You’ll go home with a nurse visit to help with the pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m hopeful this will help me eat better and gain weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. The goal is improved nutrition and fewer hospital visits. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your labs are stable—hemoglobin, electrolytes, kidney function—all good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. And my malnutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This tube is the key. With consistent feeds, your nutrition should improve over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
