conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember: call if you vomit, can’t keep fluids down, have chest pain, or fever over 101.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteral infusion is running smoothly. You’ve reached goal rate. We’re documenting this as part of your discharge process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels normal. I didn’t even notice it started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s ideal. Means your body is adjusting well. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I feel like I can manage this at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident too. Just follow the instructions, and you’ll do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You were admitted last night with left upper quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. It’s sharp, under my left rib, and goes around to my back. It gets much worse when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is this different from your usual pain from the ulcers you’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, before it was more in the middle, near my stomach. This feels higher and sharper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’re on a G-tube for feeding—any issues with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s been a little drainage around the tube for a few weeks, but it’s not painful. The feeds sometimes cause discomfort, but not as bad as eating by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. For now, we’re keeping you on bowel rest—no food or tube feeds—just IV fluids. We’ll do some tests to find the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I stop my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll keep your pantoprazole, sucralfate, and other meds. We’re giving IV fluids with vitamins and pain control as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray and a contrast study through your G-tube. No signs of a leak or blockage. Your pain isn’t from a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning an EGD—upper endoscopy—tomorrow to look at your stomach and bypass connections. That should show if there’s an ulcer or other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—we’re still reviewing your labs. White count is normal, no infection signs. We’ll proceed with the EGD tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any idea why the pain started suddenly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a new ulcer or irritation from stomach acid. The EGD will help confirm that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the EGD. We found a small 10 mm ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis—the connection from your stomach pouch to the intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m in so much pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely the cause. The rest of the intestine looked normal. We’ll start you on IV pantoprazole to reduce acid and help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart my tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try. We’re starting at your usual rate—110 mL/hr cycled. Let us know if it causes pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned increased pain with the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s worse, especially after the cycle starts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to continuous feeding at half the rate—55 mL/hr—to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still some discomfort with continuous feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, not as bad, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to a more concentrated formula at 30 mL/hr. It delivers the same calories with less volume, which may reduce irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re progressing your diet to bariatric stage 5—soft foods. Try small amounts and let us know if it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried some mashed potatoes, but the pain came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll hold oral intake for now. The tube feeds aren’t helping much either, so we’re stopping them today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then how will I get nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a PICC line tomorrow to start TPN—total parenteral nutrition—through your vein. It will give you all the nutrients you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to do a CT scan to make sure there’s no blockage or fistula causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it show the ulcer too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CT doesn’t show ulcers well, but it checks for complications like leaks or obstructions. The EGD already confirmed the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. No obstruction, no fistula, no free air. Good news. But we noticed a small pustule near your G-tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a little red, but not painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drained it and sent a culture. It may be MRSA, so we’ll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC line was placed this morning. We’re starting TPN. You’ll get all your nutrition through the line now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on this long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only until the ulcer heals and we can safely restart tube feeds. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture came back: MRSA. We’re continuing the antibiotic. The redness isn’t spreading, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s localized. We’re treating it, and you’re not running a fever, so it’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try restarting tube feeds tomorrow. The ulcer should be healing, and we need to get off TPN if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if it hurts again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. We’re switching to Peptamen Bariatric—a pre-digested formula. It’s easier to tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on Peptamen for a day. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The pain is less, especially during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re increasing to a cycled rate of 60 mL/hr. If you tolerate this, we can plan for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is minimal, you’re tolerating feeds, and your labs are stable. We’ll remove the PICC tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. You’ll go home on liquid pantoprazole twice a day, sucralfate, and your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nortriptyline? I saw it was increased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to 50 mg at night for pain control. Please let your psychiatrist know about the change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is out. You’re now fully on tube feeds and tolerating them. We’ll finalize your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. Continue Peptamen at 60 mL/hr for 12 hours, flush the tube as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the hydromorphone as needed. Call if pain worsens, or if you develop fever, vomiting, or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wash with soap and water. No dressing needed if no drainage. Call if it becomes red, swollen, or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your gastroenterologist in one week, surgeon in three. Keep all your other appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well, take your meds, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand not to take NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen. They can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll stick to acetaminophen if I need pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, avoid driving while on the hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll have someone help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we added docusate and senna for constipation. You had a lot of stool on the CT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit backed up. Thanks for catching that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send the discharge summary to your providers. You’re all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is over. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—any last questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The transport team will take you out shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One quick update—your wound culture confirmed MRSA, but it was localized and treated. No further action needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitored it closely. You’re fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over meds and feeding instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you home with services. A nurse will check in on your G-tube care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your pain service increased nortriptyline to help with chronic pain. Monitor for drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You're here because of epigastric pain that’s been going on for about a week and came back last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s in my upper left side, kind of under the ribs, and it goes around to my back. It felt a little better when I ate at first, but now it’s just dull and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and you’ve had this kind of pain before, related to your gastric bypass and ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a few times. Last time it was a marginal ulcer near the GJ anastomosis. I’ve been on Protonix and Carafate, but it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—so your stomach can rest. We’ll start IV fluids and give you medications through the IV to help with the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m not vomiting or anything. I’ve been tolerating my tube feeds just fine—60 mL per hour, 760 cc over 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear, and we’ll restart those soon. But since the pain is similar to your prior ulcers, we want to make sure we treat it aggressively from the start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What kind of treatment will I get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV pantoprazole twice a day to reduce stomach acid, and you’ll keep taking sucralfate. We’ll also give you a PCA pump for pain control so you can manage it yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used those before. But last time, narcotics made me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ll watch that closely. If the nausea returns, we may adjust the pain meds. We already ordered labs to check your iron and nutrition levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time my iron was low. I take ferrous sulfate daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs came back—your iron is 25 and ferritin is only 5, both low. We’ll adjust your supplement to a liquid form, twice a day, to help it absorb better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my other meds—should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing them. Your citalopram, quetiapine, and lorazepam are continued. But we’re consulting the chronic pain team about your nortriptyline and Effexor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Effexor’s been making me feel a bit off. If we can stop it, I’d appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team agrees. We’re stopping Effexor and increasing your nortriptyline to 100 mg at night. It may help with both nerve pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I trust my psychiatrist will get the note?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send a summary to Dr. ___ so they’re up to date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a KUB X-ray to check for free air or blockage. Good news—it’s normal. No signs of perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s probably just the ulcer acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. We’re not doing another endoscopy this time since your symptoms are classic and you’re responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been feeling nauseous again, and I dry-heaved a couple times. I think the PCA is making it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting us know. We’ll discontinue the narcotics and rely more on the nortriptyline and other non-narcotic methods. We can give you ondansetron if the nausea continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer that. I don’t want to be sick on top of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain has improved, and you’re no longer nauseous. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little sore, but manageable. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on a bariatric stage 3 diet—soft, moist foods. You’ll begin with small portions and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And can I restart my tube feeds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you’re tolerating the diet, we’ll restart your cycled feeds at 60 mL per hour for 12 hours daily, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I ate the soft foods—mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs—and I feel fine. No pain or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll keep you on the stage 3 diet and restart your tube feeds this afternoon. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. The team notes you’re ambulating well, eating without issues, and your pain is well-controlled without narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel ready to go home. What do I need to do after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the stage 3 diet and advance to stage 4 and 5 as tolerated. Keep the cycled tube feeds going. Take pantoprazole twice a day, sucralfate four times a day, and the new iron liquid twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my nortriptyline is now 100 mg at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And crush all pills before taking them—your stomach anatomy is different after bypass, so whole pills can get stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No NSAIDs, no straws, no gum—I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call your surgeon or come back if you develop fever, severe pain, vomiting, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. We’re clearing you for discharge today. You’re afebrile, pain-controlled, eating well, and ambulating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in the office to monitor your progress. We’ll send all the notes over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better and ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You're here because of left upper quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about two days ago. It’s near my g-tube site. I usually tolerate my feeds, but today I just don’t feel like eating because of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vomiting, fever, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. I haven’t had diarrhea or constipation. Just the pain and not wanting to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Roux-en-Y bypass and the g-tube in your gastric pouch, we need to check if the tube is in the right place. We’ll get some labs and likely replace the tube tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Replace it? I thought it was working fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging team wants to confirm the position. Sometimes these tubes can shift. We’ll do it under imaging guidance to make sure it’s placed correctly in the pouch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get mild sedation—fentanyl and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed. Local numbing at the site too. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. White count is slightly up but not concerning. Kidney and liver tests are normal. We’re still planning the tube replacement today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever or clear infection signs. The tenderness near the tube might be from irritation or granulation tissue. We’ll check that during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. They used silver nitrate last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. If it’s there, we’ll treat it again. Helps reduce discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to start the procedure. You’ll feel some pressure, but let us know if it’s painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Procedure is done. We successfully replaced the tube in your gastric pouch. The old one had shifted slightly. We also treated some granulation tissue with silver nitrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the new tube secure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s secured with a Flexi-Trak and the site is dressed. You should feel better soon. Pain is already improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, less pressure now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your evening labs look stable. Hemoglobin is steady, white count came down a bit. Good signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I start drinking anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with small sips. You’re tolerating oral intake so far, which is great. We’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your home meds: pantoprazole, sucralfate, nortriptyline, and the others. We’re increasing nortriptyline to 100 mg at night for better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that helped last time. What about the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that. Since the pouch connects to your esophagus, feeding through the tube might not be effective. We’re not restarting feeds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why keep the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You chose to keep it for now. We can revisit removal later. It’s there if needed, but not required for feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Pain is controlled with oral meds, you’re walking, and tolerating food. We’re planning discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any restrictions at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the tube site clean and dry. Wash with soapy water daily. No baths or swimming. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone elixir as needed, every 4 to 6 hours. But call us if pain doesn’t improve in 24 hours, or if it spreads to your chest or back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll see your surgeon soon for an endoscopy to check your anatomy. Also, continue all your vitamins and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding a lidocaine patch near the tube site for comfort. And temazepam for sleep if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home later this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes or concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I just had my gastrostomy tube removed today at the clinic, and since then I’ve been feeling really shaky, dizzy, and I had tingling in my fingers and lips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you eat anything before the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t eat all day. I was nervous about the visit, and I’ve been stressed from a trip I just got back from. I also had diarrhea during the car ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When we checked your blood sugar at the clinic, it was very low—only 35. That explains the dizziness and tingling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is that because I didn’t eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, yes. But because of your gastric bypass surgery, your body processes food and sugar differently. Skipping meals can cause your blood sugar to drop quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it could get that low. After they gave me apple juice, I felt better, but then I had cramping and diarrhea again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called ‘dumping syndrome.’ When sugar enters your intestine too fast, it can cause cramps, nausea, and diarrhea. We’ll help you avoid that going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. So why am I being admitted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your blood sugar dropped so low and you’ve been having trouble eating, we want to monitor you closely and make sure you’re stable before going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I do feel better now, but I’m still a little shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on IV fluids with some sugar to help stabilize your levels. We’ll also check your blood sugar regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Should I be worried about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a plan to prevent it. You’ll need to eat small, frequent snacks—even when you’re not hungry—especially first thing in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my diet? I was on a bariatric diet before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on Stage 1—clear liquids—and slowly advance as you tolerate it. By tomorrow, if all goes well, we’ll move you up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. I had some broth last night and didn’t feel sick. But I’ve been burping a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after surgery and with the changes in your digestion. It should improve as you start eating more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My blood sugar was 88 this morning when the nurse checked it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great improvement. We’ll keep monitoring it. We also did an X-ray this morning to make sure everything looks okay in your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small amount of contrast left from your procedure, but no signs of a blockage or free air. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Can I move up to a thicker diet today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll advance you to Stage 2 today—full liquids like yogurt and pudding. We’ll keep an eye on how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re doing well. Blood sugars are stable, and you’ve been tolerating your diet. We’re going to move you to Stage 4 today—soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I’m actually feeling hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Just remember to eat slowly and in small amounts. We also want to talk about your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking my nortriptyline and quetiapine. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those. We’re also adding pantoprazole twice a day to protect your stomach, since you’ve had ulcers in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and what about pain? I’ve had some mild discomfort at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave IV pain medication yesterday, but now you can take liquid Tylenol if needed. The pain should continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And no ibuprofen, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers. Stick to Tylenol only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re stable, eating well, and your blood sugar is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the Stage 4 diet, eat small snacks throughout the day, and check your blood sugar regularly—especially if you feel shaky or dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my blood sugar is low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eat a small snack with some carbs, wait 15 minutes, and check again. We’ve also prescribed promethazine for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and when should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have a fever, severe pain, redness or drainage from the site, or can’t keep food down. Otherwise, follow up with your surgeon in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be able to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. Ate a soft meal and my blood sugar was 92 an hour ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to crush all your pills so they’re easier to absorb, and start taking the chewable multivitamin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And no heavy lifting for six weeks, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. You can walk and do light activity, but avoid anything strenuous, especially involving your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team members. You were admitted this morning because of recurrent low blood sugar episodes, especially after your gastric bypass. We’re planning to place a gastrostomy tube today to help manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, I’ve been having those episodes more often. Will the tube help stop the lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. The idea is to test whether feeding directly into the stomach helps stabilize your blood sugar. If it does, it might support considering a reversal of your bypass later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that was an option. Is the procedure safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally safe, but like any surgery, there are risks. We started laparoscopically, but had to convert to open due to some scar tissue. We placed the tube and repaired a small colotomy we found. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember waking up in the recovery room. My belly feels sore, but I’m alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’re on a PCA pump for pain with hydromorphone. We’ll switch to oral meds soon. You’re doing well neurologically and breathing fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your labs are stable. Blood sugar was 112 this morning, which is good. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about crashing again. Can I eat anything yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re starting you on clear liquids tomorrow. Your stomach and bowels need time to wake up after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re on a Stage 5 bariatric diet today—soft foods. Try small bites and chew well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. My belly feels a little bloated though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. We’ll get an X-ray to check for ileus—when the bowels slow down after surgery. It’s common and usually temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows post-op ileus. There’s no movement of contrast through your bowels. We’ll hold oral intake for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t eat anything? How long will this last?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It varies. We’ll encourage walking and use of the incentive spirometer. Most people improve in a few days. We’ll repeat the X-ray to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat X-ray shows no change yet. We’re still seeing distention. But no free air, so no leak. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t passed gas much. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, reduced gas and bowel movements are typical with ileus. We gave a suppository, but it didn’t work. We’ll keep supporting you and wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your abdomen is less distended this morning. You passed gas and had a small bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a bit better. Does that mean I can eat again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on oral intake for now. But we’re planning to start tube feedings tomorrow. That’s the goal of the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll connect a feeding bag to your tube. The formula is high-protein, moderate-carb. It runs slowly through a pump, 24/7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feedings today at a low rate. We’ll increase it gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still take my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue acarbose and pramlintide with meals. We’re monitoring your blood sugar every few hours to make sure it stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood sugars are staying between 100 and 130. No hypoglycemia. We’ll keep advancing the feeding rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I haven’t felt shaky or dizzy at all today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. White count is a bit high, but that’s expected after surgery. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been walking a little more each day. My pain is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re on oral oxycodone now, and we’ll taper that soon. You’re also on omeprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I was on pantoprazole before. Why the switch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole is similar and works well with your other meds. We’ll keep it for now to prevent ulcers, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating full tube feedings. Blood sugars remain stable. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How do I manage the tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep the feedings running 24/7. Flush the tube with 100 mL water every 8 hours. We’ll send a nurse to help you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I have problems with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you can’t flush it, if there’s leakage, or if you have nausea, vomiting, or distention. Also check residuals before feeding—if more than 50 mL, stop and call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? Should I check it more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—before and after meals, at bedtime, and if you feel shaky. We want to see if the tube feedings are helping prevent lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home meds except we’ve added docusate and bisacodyl to help prevent constipation from the pain meds and tube feedings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take those. When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ in two weeks. They’ll evaluate your response to the tube and discuss next steps, possibly reversal surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful this helps. I’m tired of living in fear of passing out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful too. This is a big step. You’ve done really well—ambulating, no fever, pain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final check—vitals are stable, wound looks clean, you’re passing gas, and feedings are going well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. A little nervous, but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions with you. Call if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, vomiting, or tube issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my blood sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check it immediately. If it’s low, stop the tube feeding and call us. We may need to adjust the rate or formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You handled this surgery and recovery really well. We’re discharging you home with visiting nurse support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll rest, walk daily, and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up the good work. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new pain or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just a little sore at the incision, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Keep using the oral pain med as needed. Avoid heavy lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll have my husband help with chores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And remember—flush the tube every 8 hours, even if not feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 100 mL of water. I’ve been practicing with the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re all set. We’ll call you tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. I see you’re here because your surgical wound hasn’t healed properly after your gastrostomy tube surgery. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the top part of my incision keeps draining, even though the skin looked like it closed. It’s been like this for weeks, and it just won’t heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We were concerned that a retained suture might be causing the problem, which can act like a foreign body and prevent healing. That’s why we brought you in today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so something was left inside? That could be causing the drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Sometimes a stitch can erode or react with the tissue, leading to a small tunnel that keeps draining. We took care of it earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, you already did something? I just got to my room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were taken to the operating room this morning. We reopened the wound, cleaned out the area, and removed a small piece of suture that was causing the issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it happened already. How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It went well. The procedure was straightforward. We debrided the area to remove unhealthy tissue and made sure the cavity is clean. You’re healing well otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s your pain? Are you comfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little sore, but not bad. Better than before, actually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep you on oral pain medication as needed. We also started you on antibiotics to prevent infection after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics? Is there an infection now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a full infection, but there was some inflammation and drainage, so we’re being cautious. The antibiotics will help clear any bacteria and support healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well overnight—no fever, stable vitals, and your pain is controlled. We’d like to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to pack the wound with a clean dressing twice a day. We’ll give you supplies. Also, finish the full 7-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other medications? Should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your regular medications unless we told you otherwise. Especially the Symlin and acarbose for your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a follow-up appointment scheduled in a few days. They’ll check your wound and guide the next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for any warning signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call if you develop fever, increased redness or swelling, worsening pain, or if you can’t keep fluids down. Also, avoid heavy lifting for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. We’ll get the discharge papers ready, and a nurse will go over the dressing instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any questions before we send you home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Dressing twice a day, antibiotics for a week, keep taking my regular meds, and call if anything gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You’re here because you had sudden abdominal pain after stepping on your feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I tripped on the tube three days ago, felt a sharp tug, and the pain hasn’t gone away. The area around the tube is also more red and has this yellow discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And are you having nausea, vomiting, or any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or vomiting. Feeds are going in okay, but the skin around the tube is really irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—no tube feeds—just to be safe. We’ll start IV fluids and get some imaging to make sure the tube hasn’t moved or caused a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they do that tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the radiology team is already setting up a G-tube study. They’ll inject a little contrast to see where it goes and check if there’s any leakage outside the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the scan is back. The tube is in the right place, and the contrast went straight into your stomach and then into the small bowel. No signs of a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So nothing tore or came loose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the internal part looks intact. But we did see some irritation and granulation tissue at the skin site, which is likely why it’s painful and draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same thing that happened before, when they found a suture stuck in the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, but this time it’s not a foreign body. It’s just the body’s way of healing—sometimes too much tissue forms. We’ll manage it with better wound care and frequent dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are normal—no infection signs. We’re going to restart your tube feeds slowly and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s better, but still there when I touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you pain meds as needed. The discomfort should improve as the skin irritation resolves. The redness has already gotten much better with proper care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating the feeds well, no nausea, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Should I do anything different at home with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing frequent dressing changes, and watch for increased redness, swelling, or foul-smelling discharge. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in two weeks—he may consider repositioning the tube if the granulation tissue persists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and I can keep taking my regular medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are continued, including the mupirocin for MRSA and your vitamins. We’re adding a stool softener to help with bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried something serious happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re stable, healing, and safe to go home. Just call if you develop fever, severe pain, or trouble with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. You’ll get written instructions and prescriptions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to keep the site clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with the follow-up. We want to make sure this doesn’t keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Still doing well? No new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still feeling okay. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the bariatric team doctors. You came in tonight because of low blood sugar—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning feeling really shaky and confused. My glucose monitor alarm went off—it said my blood sugar was 43.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s quite low. Did you treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my sugar pills right away. I felt better after a few minutes, but then it happened again later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’re going to keep an eye on your levels. You also mentioned increased drainage around your G-tube and some pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the site has been leaking more than usual. I’m changing the dressing twice a day now because it gets soaked. And it’s tender—more than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. We’ve ordered a scan to make sure your tube is still in the right place and not leaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it possible the feeds are backing up into the bag? I’ve been worried the pump isn’t delivering them properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. The scan will help us see how the contrast moves. If it’s refluxing, we’ll adjust your setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your abdominal X-ray with contrast shows the G-tube is correctly placed in the stomach. No leakage outside the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube is okay? But why am I having these lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube is working, but we think your hypoglycemia might be related to bacterial overgrowth in your intestines. You’ve had that before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from my breath test. So that could be causing the lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Bacteria can ferment carbs and trigger insulin release. We’re restarting your Flagyl to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the soreness at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some granulation tissue—extra tissue that sometimes grows around tubes. It can cause irritation and drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s common. We’ll treat it with silver nitrate to reduce it and prescribe an ointment called Bactroban to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugars have been stable overnight—between 80 and 110. No episodes of hypoglycemia so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the Flagyl is working already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s early, but staying on your feeds and being in a controlled setting helps. Your endocrinologist wants a fasting test to check what’s driving the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fasting test? But I need my tube feeds to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it carefully. We’ll stop the feeds and monitor your blood sugar every hour. When it drops to around 55, we’ll draw blood to check insulin, C-peptide, and other levels, then restart your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And that will tell us why I’m having lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It helps distinguish if it’s from too much insulin production, reactive hypoglycemia, or something else. Your endocrinologist will review the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the fasting test this morning. You went about 12 hours without feeds. Your blood sugar dropped to 55, and we got the labs right then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do? Did I pass out or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you stayed alert the whole time. Nurses checked you every hour. All the labs were sent to your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And the contrast study this morning—what did that show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The contrast moved all the way into your colon and rectum. That means your digestive tract is open and functioning—no blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s moving like it should?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your tube site is looking better after treatment. We’ll keep using the silver nitrate and Bactroban ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Another good night—your sugars stayed between 55 and 110. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your tube feeds as before. Take Flagyl three times a day for the bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds—octreotide and acarbose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Octreotide helps reduce insulin spikes, and acarbose slows sugar absorption. They may help prevent lows after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Apply the Bactroban ointment twice a day to the granulation tissue. Keep the dressing clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll review your test results and adjust your plan if needed. We’ll send them all the labs from the fasting test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—vitals stable, sugars in range. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds as prescribed. Use glucose tablets if your sugar drops. And call if you have fever, redness, or increased pain at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel shaky again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your sugar. If it’s low, treat it with glucose and sit down. If it doesn’t improve, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel much better knowing we’re on top of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send prescriptions for Flagyl, Bactroban, and the new meds. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one more thing—should I keep checking my blood sugar at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially before meals and at bedtime. And any time you feel shaky or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be overseeing your care during this admission. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having more frequent low blood sugar episodes—almost daily—and I keep getting confused. I even sent an email to my specialist that I don’t remember writing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds concerning. These episodes—do they come with dizziness, memory loss, or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of those. And I’ve been dry heaving a lot, though not actually vomiting. My stomach pain has come back too, like the ulcers I had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You're on diazoxide now instead of octreotide, and your tube feeds were adjusted recently. But things aren’t improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I was doing well until I came back from my trip. Then the lows started again, and the constipation returned even though I’m eating high-fiber foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your G-tube site, run some labs, and consult neurology and endocrinology. Your symptoms could be tied to hypoglycemia, but we need to rule out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly an endoscopy to check for ulcers or other issues in your stomach. But first, we’ll monitor your glucose and adjust your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back normal—no infection, liver issues, or electrolyte imbalances. Glucose was 93, which is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, but I’m still worried about the lows happening without warning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch your tube feeding schedule. Instead of continuous, we’ll cycle them—20 during the day, 40 at night—to see if that helps stabilize your sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the nausea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re also changing your anti-nausea med from Zofran to Compazine, which may work better for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case. They don’t think you’re having seizures. Your confusion and memory lapses are likely due to the hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. But how do we stop the lows from happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a monitored fast tomorrow. We’ll stop daytime feeds around 1 PM and check your glucose. If it drops below 55, we’ll draw special labs to understand what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if it doesn’t drop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we’ll know your body is maintaining sugar okay during fasting, and we can focus on adjusting meds and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any symptoms overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lows, actually. I did have some dry heaving, but not as bad as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your fingerstick this morning was 88. We’ll start the fasting study today at 1 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping your daytime tube feeds now. We’ll check your glucose every 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose is holding at 78. That’s well above the threshold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no labs today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. But we noticed your glucose meter readings were inconsistent with actual fingersticks. We’ve replaced the meter and strips to ensure accuracy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it could be off. That might explain some of the scary lows I thought I was having.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want you to have reliable tools. We’ll also schedule an endoscopy tomorrow to check your stomach and bypass anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the endoscopy this morning. The good news is no ulcers were found at the gastrojejunal anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the abnormal mucosa they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are some changes in the esophagus and stomach lining, but nothing urgent. We’ll continue your pantoprazole twice daily to protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the metronidazole for bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it for now. The GI team felt it wasn’t clearly helping, and we want to simplify your regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team met with you, right? They went over adding complex carbohydrates by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they suggested oatmeal, whole grains—things that digest slowly. I think I can manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That, combined with nighttime tube feeds only, should help prevent rapid glucose swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose has stayed above 78 the entire time. No episodes of hypoglycemia in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s really encouraging. Does this mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll finalize your new medication and feeding plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your mental status is clear, and you’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes should I expect in my routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll run tube feeds only at night—from 11 PM to 7 AM—at a rate of 40. During the day, you’ll eat complex carbs and avoid simple sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Diazoxide will now be taken three times a day—25 mg at breakfast, 25 mg at dinner, and 50 mg at bedtime. We’re also switching your sleep med to zolpidem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have prochlorperazine—5 mg up to four times a day as needed. Take it at the first sign of nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ in three weeks. Call sooner if you have severe lows, persistent nausea, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much more confident about managing this now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here if you need us. Take care, and follow the plan closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—your G-tube site looks stable. The hypergranulation tissue is still there, but not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I continue the mupirocin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, apply it twice daily as before. If it gets worse, let your surgeon know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. The nurse will go over everything, including your new feeding schedule and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to review it all before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your mental clarity has improved significantly. That’s likely because your glucose is stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. I hope this continues at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. Stick to the plan, monitor your sugar with the new meter, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you home in about an hour. Do you have any final questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand when to take each dose of diazoxide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—25 mg with breakfast, 25 mg with dinner, and 50 mg at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember, the nighttime tube feeds start at 11 PM, rate 40, until 7 AM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve written it down to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. We’re discharging you now. Please follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having diarrhea and feeling dehydrated. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had diarrhea for about three days now. It started with cramping in my lower belly, then loose stools. No blood, but I’ve been sweating, feeling chills, and my mouth is dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been trying to stay hydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been drinking fluids and using saline flushes through my G-tube, but it hasn’t been enough. I came in this morning after my last bowel movement because I just felt so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help with the dehydration. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—for a few hours to give your gut some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but what about my tube feeds? I usually get them at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your tube feeds later, once we’re sure you’re stable. Right now, we’re focusing on rehydration and seeing if your symptoms settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had C. diff before—could this be that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, which is why we need a stool sample to check. You haven’t had a bowel movement since arriving, so we’re waiting for one to test for C. diff and other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I hope it’s not C. diff again—that was rough last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll know more once we get the test back. In the meantime, your labs look stable—your glucose is 102, which is good, and your electrolytes are mostly normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on diazoxide for the hypoglycemia. Should I keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your diazoxide. We’re monitoring your glucose closely. So far, it’s staying in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been anxious—should I take my lorazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take it as prescribed—1 mg twice a day. Let the nurse know if you’re feeling particularly anxious, and we can adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I also take nortriptyline and quetiapine at night—should I take those later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you those with your evening meds. We’re reviewing all your medications to make sure they’re appropriate during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea too, off and on. Can I take something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use prochlorperazine 5 mg every six hours as needed. We’ll hold the ondansetron for now since you’re NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pantoprazole? I take that twice a day for reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that. Even though you’re not eating, it helps protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You passed a stool last night—thank you. We sent it for C. diff testing. Also, your abdominal X-ray from yesterday showed no blockage, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any idea what’s causing the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be bacterial overgrowth—we’ve seen that before with your history. Or it could be related to your gastric bypass. We’re restarting your tube feeds today to see how you tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was here, they changed my diet to complex carbs. Should I be doing that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you on that plan—complex carbs, low sugar. It helps prevent dumping syndrome and hypoglycemia. The nutrition team will adjust your tube feed formula accordingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When will I know about the C. diff test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Results should be back by this afternoon. If it’s negative, we may still treat you with metronidazole, given your history of C. diff and bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate it well. Some get mild nausea or a metallic taste. Rarely, it can cause dizziness. Let us know if you feel anything unusual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tube feeds were well tolerated this morning. We’re also starting an enteral infusion of concentrated nutrition to help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’m feeling less tired already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your dehydration is improving. We’re also starting metronidazole—500 mg every eight hours—for five days, just to cover any bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the C. diff test came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was negative. But given your history, we’re being cautious. This will also help with the small bowel overgrowth we’ve seen before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust your judgment. Should I continue the pantoprazole while on metronidazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking it. It doesn’t interact with metronidazole and helps with your reflux history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. No more diarrhea, you’re tolerating feeds, and you’re well hydrated. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What meds should I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lorazepam for anxiety, nortriptyline and quetiapine at night, pantoprazole twice a day, and prochlorperazine as needed for nausea. And finish the full course of metronidazole—three times a day for five days.
