conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the zolpidem? I see it’s on the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg at bedtime if you’re having trouble sleeping. But avoid alcohol while on metronidazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—follow up with your bariatric team. They’ll monitor your hypoglycemia and adjust your diazoxide if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Keep up with the complex carb diet, stay hydrated, and call if the diarrhea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some bloating and changes in your G-tube output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. My tube output has been brown and sometimes green or yellow. It’s also increased a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you mentioned feeling distended after your last tube feed at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt really bloated and uncomfortable. I haven’t had any fever or vomiting, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. No diarrhea either?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and gastric bypass, we’re concerned this could be a recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Could the antibiotics I’ve been giving through the tube be affecting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll hold off on tube feeds for now and start IV fluids to let your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also start you on IV Zosyn to cover for possible infection while we run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on that the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess based on your response. First, we’ll do a plain X-ray to check your bowel gas pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The KUB came back. Good news — no signs of obstruction or free air. Your G-tube is in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also do a contrast study tomorrow morning to confirm the tube is functioning properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and what about the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a soap enema every six hours to help relieve distention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The G-tube study with contrast was successful. The tube is patent and correctly placed in the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, so it’s not misplaced?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s where it should be. No leakage either. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the bacteria in the fluid? I saw something about mixed flora.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did see mixed bacterial flora in the fluid sample, but no anaerobes were isolated. It supports the idea of bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is that why the output changed color?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be contributing. We’re switching from IV Zosyn to IV Ceftriaxone and Flagyl to better target gut bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Flagyl at home. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You’ll continue oral Flagyl after discharge as part of your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And can I start eating or using the tube again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart your tube feeds slowly and advance your diet to bariatric stage 5 today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tolerated that before. Should I expect nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. You can use ondansetron if needed, but so far you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The bloating has gone down, and I haven’t had any discomfort with the feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your labs are stable — no fever, normal white count, and lactate is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood cultures were negative?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both sets came back with no growth. That rules out a bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about C. diff? I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stool test was negative for C. difficile and other pathogens like Salmonella or Shigella.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infectious diarrhea then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like bacterial overgrowth is the main issue, not an acute infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well overnight. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the stage 5 bariatric diet. Don’t advance it on your own. And call the clinic tomorrow to confirm when to restart tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking Flagyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue Flagyl 500 mg every 8 hours. We’ve given you a prescription to refill it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I avoid anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen — they can cause ulcers. And no straws or gum to reduce air swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or return if you get a fever over 101.5, severe pain, vomiting, or can’t eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with my bariatric team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll coordinate your ongoing care. You’re doing well — just keep up the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. We'll get your discharge papers ready shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check — still no pain, eating well, and moving around okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything feels back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge is approved. Take care and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when she is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain and some low blood sugars. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain started a few days ago—mostly in my lower belly. It’s dull but constant. And I’ve been feeling shaky, which I know means my sugar is dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are you checking your glucose regularly? And when you feel shaky, are you treating it right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have my continuous monitor, but I usually wait until it alarms before I take sugar. I didn’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be part of the problem. We recommend treating when you see a downward trend, not waiting for the alarm. We’ll talk more about that later. For now, we’re going to run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve also been nauseous, but no vomiting. Still taking my tube feeds as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cortisol came back elevated, but that can happen with stress. Your glucose was normal this morning at 88, and your lipase was slightly high but not concerning for pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired? Could it be my adrenal glands?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The cortisol is probably reactive. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s not the main issue right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound of your right upper quadrant is back. Good news—no gallstones, no liver issues. That rules out a few things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be my gallbladder again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same here. We also did an abdominal X-ray. It shows some stool buildup in your colon, but no blockage. Your G-tube is in good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on more lactulose lately—my doctor increased the dose. I’ve had looser stools, but maybe not enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely helping. We won’t change it now. But we did find something else—your urine test shows a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I haven’t had burning or urgency. Just the belly pain and low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes UTIs present atypically, especially with your history. We’re going to start you on oral Bactrim to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you a dose of tube feeding just now to keep your nutrition on track. You’re tolerating it well, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried I might need to stop feeds again like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. You’re not vomiting, and your abdomen isn’t distended. We’ll keep you on liquids by mouth only for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endocrinology team reviewed your case. They agree—you should treat low sugars as soon as the trend starts, not wait for the alarm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So if I see it going down, I should drink juice or eat something sweet right then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That can prevent the full drop and reduce your risk of shaking or even passing out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize that made such a difference. I’ll start doing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. Pain improved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much less pain today. Still some tenderness, but not constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable, and you’ve had no fevers. The Bactrim is working on the UTI. We’ll keep you on it for a full five-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Bactrim twice a day, right? And I keep taking my Flagyl for the bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. The Flagyl helps with your small bowel overgrowth, and we don’t want to stop it abruptly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if you keep improving. Any concerns before we go over the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to drive? I don’t want to ask someone to pick me up if I’m not cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert and coherent, so yes, you can drive. But if you feel any dizziness, pull over and treat your sugar immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I should keep following up with my endocrinologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and reschedule with your psychologist too. Mental health is part of managing chronic conditions like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Final check before discharge. Abdomen soft, no fever, walking independently. We’ll send you home with a few things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What medications will I be taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds: Flagyl, lactulose, pantoprazole, and your psychiatric medications. Plus, Bactrim twice daily for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a small supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but use it sparingly. Tylenol is safer for you long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And tube feeds—continue as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And remember: no solid foods by mouth. Liquids only. And trend your glucose—treat early, not late.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll practice that. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if the pain returns, you develop a fever, or have trouble with your G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. Nurse will go over the written instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check. Any new symptoms? Pain? Nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling steady. Sugar levels have been better since I started treating earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. You’re doing exactly what you should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I came in. I didn’t realize the UTI could be causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infections can trigger a lot, especially with your history. We’re glad we caught it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with my PCP and psychologist like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe and keep monitoring those sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling confused and having low blood sugar episodes. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been tired, sweating a lot, and confused—especially after eating. I think it’s because my body isn’t absorbing my meds or nutrients right after my gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You mentioned your Seroquel levels were low despite high doses. We’ll check your absorption and run some labs to see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ammonia was high two weeks ago. They gave me Rifaximin, but I’m still not feeling right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed that. Your initial ammonia was normal today, but we’ll monitor it closely. We’ll also check liver function and look for metabolic causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this confusion be from my liver? I’ve had fatty liver in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your liver enzymes are normal now. We’ll get a full workup, including an MRI and EEG, to rule out other causes like seizures or brain lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring. What about my low blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology will evaluate that. We suspect it might be due to overproduction of insulin after meals, which can happen after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not just from my tube feeds being off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your tube feeds running for now. But we may do a fasting test to see how your body handles low intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ammonia level rose to 52 yesterday. We’re concerned this could be contributing to your confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: High ammonia can affect brain function. It’s often from liver issues, but your liver looks okay. We’re considering a rare genetic issue in your metabolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A genetic problem? Like something I was born with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re sending a urea cycle panel after a 12-hour fast to check for that. It’s rare, but it fits your symptoms after high-protein meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel worse after eating meat. So that could be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll test that theory. For now, we’ll keep you on clear liquids and continue your tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to hold your tube feeds overnight for a fasting test. Endocrinology wants to check your insulin levels when you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get low blood sugar again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. If your glucose drops, we’ll treat it right away. This test helps us see if your body is making too much insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. But please wake me if I seem confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you didn’t become hypoglycemic overnight. Your insulin, C-peptide, and beta-hydroxybutyrate were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my insulin causing lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not during fasting. But it could still be happening after meals. Endocrinology recommends continuing continuous tube feeds and avoiding food by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no eating at all? Not even a cracker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing with calories. Water is fine. Eating could trigger dumping syndrome or insulin spikes. We want to keep your glucose stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hepatology saw you today. They don’t think you have cirrhosis or hepatic encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They think it’s related to your gastric bypass anatomy. A high-protein meal may overwhelm your metabolism, especially if there’s a urea cycle issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a test today. You’ll have a high-protein meal, and we’ll draw blood every 30 minutes to check ammonia and liver enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some symptoms, like confusion or nausea, but we’ll be right here. It’s important we capture what happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After your meal, your AST and ALT went up, and your ammonia peaked at 52. You had slurred speech and tremors, but they improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much after lunch. That scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called transient confusion. It’s likely due to the protein load. The good news is your MRI and EEG were normal—no seizures or brain lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my brain, it’s my metabolism?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re waiting on the urea cycle panel. If that’s normal, we’ll consider other metabolic pathways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge is coming up. Your ammonia is down to 23, and you’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are we any closer to an answer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think your symptoms are due to post-gastric bypass changes. The high-protein meal test confirmed that. A genetic urea cycle defect is still possible—results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the low blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology thinks it’s dumping syndrome—rapid food movement into the intestine causing insulin surge. That’s why we’re keeping you on tube feeds only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? I take Rifaximin for bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Rifaximin three times a day. We don’t think SIBO is the main issue, but it’s safe to keep it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver team recommends switching your tube feed formula to NutriHep, which is easier on your metabolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s designed for people with liver or metabolic issues. It has balanced protein and calories to avoid overwhelming your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when will I get the new formula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s being arranged. Until then, stay on your current feeds at 65cc/hr. You have follow-ups with your PCP, endocrinologist, and surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Continue tube feeds, no oral intake, and follow up in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you when the urea cycle and pro-insulin results come in. Call us if you have confusion, low sugar, or can’t keep feeds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take care, and we’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with abdominal pain, nausea, and some diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had this dull, constant pain in my upper belly for about a day. It’s different from my usual G-tube site pain. Feels more like the ulcers I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of gastric bypass and previous marginal ulcers, we need to check if it’s ulcer-related again. We’ve done some blood work and an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My lipase was high last time—was it high again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lipase was elevated—186, which is about three times the upper limit. That raised concern for pancreatitis, but your symptoms and history make us also think about ulcers or bowel overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had dumping syndrome and bacterial overgrowth before. Could that be flaring up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That’s part of our differential. The X-ray showed no free air or obstruction, which is good. But your bladder was very full—possibly contributing to discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t felt the urge to go. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it. No need for a catheter unless it persists. For now, we’re starting IV fluids and holding your tube feeds temporarily—bowel rest—to see if your pancreas settles down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? It’s still pretty constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you dilaudid in the ER, and we’ll continue with pain meds as needed. We’re also starting a proton-pump inhibitor to protect your stomach lining, just in case it’s an ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs are stable, and your lipase has already dropped to 118. That’s a good sign. We’re still concerned about the cause, so we’ve scheduled an MRCP tomorrow to look at your pancreas and bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an MRI? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a special MRI that focuses on the pancreas and bile system. It will help us rule out gallstones or inflammation. We’ll also give you some oral contrast through your G-tube to check for dumping syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it show if I have another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: MRCP isn’t the best for ulcers. If we’re still suspicious, we may do an EGD—a scope down through your stomach—to look directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRCP results are back. Good news—your pancreas and bile ducts look completely normal. No signs of inflammation or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The elevated lipase might be from your medications—fluoxetine has a small risk. But your symptoms still point to possible ulcer. We’re scheduling an EGD this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a few of those. Will they treat anything they find?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If there’s an ulcer, they can cauterize it if it’s bleeding or has a lesion. We’ll also restart your tube feeds after, using a low-protein formula to avoid stressing your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time—high protein made me confused. Is that still a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your prior workup suggested a possible urea cycle issue. We’re still waiting on genetic results, but we’ll keep protein low for now to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Your EGD is done. You had a marginal ulcer near the gastric bypass site, and there was a small pigmented lesion. It’s been cauterized, so it should heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No biopsy was taken, but the appearance wasn’t concerning. Still, we’ll repeat the EGD in 8 weeks to make sure it’s healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your pantoprazole to twice daily and adding sucralfate four times a day. That helps protect the ulcer site. You’ll take the sucralfate by mouth, not through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it coats the upper stomach and esophagus better when swallowed. It helps form a protective layer over the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Can I restart my tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting them now—low protein NutriHep, continuous drip. We’ll monitor for nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any pain or nausea since restarting feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Pain is down to a 3. Still a little bloated, but no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs today also look better—lipase is normal, and your kidney function is good. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need pain meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a short course of oxycodone for breakthrough pain. But we’ll also start a bowel regimen—senna and docusate—since narcotics can cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I’ll take them as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your fluoxetine and atenolol are continuing. No changes there. And we’ll keep rifaximin for bacterial overgrowth prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about H. pylori? Should I be tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI wants a stool antigen test, but you haven’t had a bowel movement this admission. Please follow up with them in clinic to get it done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done really well overnight—no pain, tolerating feeds, vitals stable. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times a day by mouth. Keep using NutriHep with low protein. Take oxycodone only if needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, senna and docusate twice daily while on oxycodone. They’ll help prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see GI again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In 8 weeks for a repeat EGD. They’ll check how the ulcer is healing. Call sooner if you have severe pain, vomiting, or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve made great progress. We’ll send all instructions to your husband. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. Can you tell me about the pain you’ve been having?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. It’s that same epigastric pain I had last time—right in the upper middle part of my belly. It started four days ago, and I’ve been nauseous and vomiting this dark yellow fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are you running any fevers, or have you noticed blood in your vomit or stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers, no blood. I haven’t had diarrhea or constipation either. I passed stool this morning, and I’m passing gas normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re on continuous tube feeds, correct? And still NPO by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t eaten anything by mouth. I’ve been doing the tube feeds around the clock and flushing with water every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And how’s your blood sugar been? Any episodes of low sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it’s been stable. No hypoglycemia since I’ve been here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. We’re going to start you on IV fluids and some IV pantoprazole to help with the ulcer. We also gave you some IV meds for nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been taking my pantoprazole and sucralfate at home. I even switched to liquid omeprazole yesterday because we thought the pill wasn’t absorbing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you’re consistent. Sometimes after gastric bypass, pill absorption can be unreliable. We’ll keep you on IV pantoprazole for now to make sure we’re getting strong acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Do you think it’s another marginal ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and symptoms, yes, that’s the most likely cause. But we need to rule out serious complications like a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. How do you check for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a chest X-ray and an abdominal X-ray to look for free air, which would suggest a hole in the stomach or intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back. No signs of free air under the diaphragm, and your lungs look clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means there’s no perforation. We’re also waiting on the abdominal X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray is also clear—no obstruction or free air. There’s a bit of stool buildup, but nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at this time. You’re stable, pain is improving with the IV meds, and no signs of complications. We’ll keep you on IV pantoprazole and continue your tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also noticed a little more drainage around my G-tube site this morning. It’s not red or painful, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for mentioning that. We’ll check the site. Since you have a history of MRSA, we’ll keep an eye on it for infection, but no signs now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I haven’t needed any pain meds since last night, and no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs from yesterday were normal—white count is fine, no signs of infection or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the lipase? Last time it was high and we worried about pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase was 38—well within normal. No concern for pancreatitis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So it’s really just the ulcer flaring up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks that way. We’re going to keep you on the IV pantoprazole for another day, then transition you back to oral meds before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I stay on the liquid omeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we’re switching you to lansoprazole oral disintegrating tablet—dissolves on the tongue, no need to swallow. Should absorb better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds easier. And sucralfate still four times a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue sucralfate via the tube, one gram four times a day. It coats the ulcer and helps it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really well. No pain, no nausea. Still doing the tube feeds without any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll plan to discharge you tomorrow if you continue to do this well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Do I need another endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your symptoms are improving without it, and no signs of bleeding or perforation. But you should follow up with GI in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I have an appointment already scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. We’ll send you home with lansoprazole, sucralfate, and your other usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue continuous feeds, nothing by mouth, and keep up with the water flushes every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the drainage at the G-tube site? Should I do anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the area clean and dry. We’re prescribing mupirocin ointment twice a day since you’re MRSA-positive, just to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take hydrocodone every four hours as needed for pain. But try the non-medication methods first—distraction, positioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Keep taking your meds, continue tube feeds, and follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if the pain comes back, or if you develop fever, vomiting, or issues with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll keep that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having this pain in my upper belly, mostly on the right side and near my stomach. It’s worse the last two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it different from your usual G-tube pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this feels deeper, more like a burning in my upper belly. It reminds me of when I had that ulcer before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you ran out of oxycodone—have you taken anything for the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just Tylenol, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll get you something for pain. You’re still on your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at 40 cc/hour. No vomiting or diarrhea. But I think the feed is leaking around the tube a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check the site. Any fever, chills, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to keep you on bowel rest for now, give you IV fluids, and start a medication called pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid. We also ordered an ultrasound of your gallbladder and liver to rule out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had that ultrasound before—last time it was fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we just got the results. No gallstones or gallbladder inflammation. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we think it might be a recurrence of your marginal ulcer—the kind that can happen after gastric bypass. That’s why we’re using the acid blocker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I’ve been stressed lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stress can play a role. We’ll also check your labs to make sure there’s no infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white blood cell count was a bit high yesterday evening but came down. Liver and pancreas enzymes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rise could be from inflammation or stress on the body. But no fever, and your other markers look good. We don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lactate was high—what does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was mildly elevated, which can happen with pain or dehydration. It’s improving, so we’re not concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Can I start drinking water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on small sips. And we’re adding a medication called sucralfate—it coats the ulcer and helps it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s often used for ulcers like yours. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole for now and transition to oral meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I haven’t needed any strong pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll restart your tube feeds at 50 cc/hour and keep you on water by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube—I’m supposed to get it replaced soon, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your surgeon has scheduled the revision. We’re making sure the ulcer is under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious about it. I feel like it’s taking forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We want to do it safely, especially with the ulcer. But you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your pain has improved, and you’re tolerating feeds and water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue lansoprazole twice daily, sucralfate four times a day, and oxycodone liquid for breakthrough pain. Also, keep taking your fluoxetine, rifaximin, and other home meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, NutriHep at 50 cc/hour. Monitor the G-tube site for redness, swelling, or increased pain. Call your surgeon if you notice anything unusual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as needed. But if it’s not helping, or if you have fever, vomiting, or severe bloating, go to the ER or call your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll keep avoiding NSAIDs, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No NSAIDs, alcohol, or smoking. They can worsen ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up, and your G-tube surgery is coming up soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. I understand you’ve been having ongoing pain with your G-tube. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bothering me. The tube pulled at some point, and the pain never went away. It’s constant around the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had several G-tubes placed before, and this one is in your remnant stomach. We discussed re-siting the tube, and you’ve decided to go ahead with that today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want more major surgery like revising the bypass or dealing with the pancreas. I just want the tube moved to stop the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The plan is to remove the current tube and place a new one surgically through an open procedure. It’s low risk, and we expect good relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? I’m a little nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be fully under general anesthesia. The anesthesia team will monitor you closely the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you — you’ve just come out of surgery. The open G-tube replacement went smoothly. No complications. You’re in the recovery area now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, already? I didn’t feel a thing. Is the new tube in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the new tube is securely placed in a better location. You’ll stay on pain medication through the tube for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt when I wake up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have some discomfort, but we’re using a PCA pump at first, then switch to Dilaudid tablets through the tube. Pain should be well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 5. It’s sore, but not sharp. Better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s expected. You’re doing well — heart rate and breathing are stable. We’ll keep watching you tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll stay NPO tonight. We’ll start tube feeds tomorrow once we’re sure everything is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look good — no signs of infection or bleeding. We’re going to start your tube feeds today at a low rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I was worried about not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting nutrition through the new tube. We’ll ramp up slowly to your usual 65 mL/hour. You’ll stay on Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Like fluoxetine and pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll crush all your pills and give them through the G-tube once you’re tolerating feeds. No NSAIDs — you’re allergic, remember?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, no ibuprofen. I’ll stick to acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRSA screen came back — no MRSA detected. That’s excellent. Means lower infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had it before, so I was worried. Good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is down, you’re tolerating full feeds at 65 mL/hour, and you walked in the hall this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is maybe a 2 now. And I feel stronger walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll keep encouraging movement to prevent clots. You’re on heparin shots and compression boots for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the wound healing okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the incision is clean, no redness or drainage. You’ll have a nurse come daily to change the dressing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another good night. You’re afebrile, pain is controlled, and you’re passing gas — all signs your gut is working normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have a little water by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll let you sip water. But keep all nutrition through the tube. No solid food by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds — I need to crush them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Crush all pills and mix with water before flushing through the tube. That’s critical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re stable, ambulating, and tolerating everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you get a fever over 101.5, severe pain, redness or pus from the wound, or can’t keep feeds running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? I have the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. It can make you drowsy, so no driving or heavy lifting over 10 pounds for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have help at home. The nurse will come daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will visit daily for dressing changes. Keep the site clean and dry. You can shower, but no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check — you’re afebrile, pain is mild, and you’re eating and drinking small amounts safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Discharge meds include acetaminophen, Dilaudid, and stool softeners for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take Colace twice a day, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and bisacodyl if needed. Keep up the fluids and movement. Follow up with your surgeon in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no NSAIDs — I remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve got it. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you understand to crush all pills and give via G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll crush them and flush well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if the tube clogs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Flush with warm water, and if it doesn’t clear, call the nurse or doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. We’re discharging you with home health support. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m so glad the pain is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your tube feeds should stay at 65 mL/hour continuously. Don’t adjust the rate unless instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Nutrihep at 65 mL/hour, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And keep taking pantoprazole and rifaximin as prescribed — they help with stomach acid and gut bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. I’ve been on them a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, your depression and anxiety meds — fluoxetine and zolpidem — keep those consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take fluoxetine three times a day and zolpidem at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. And clonidine patch once a week. All these go through the G-tube, crushed or dissolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my caregiver knows the routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re well prepared. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for fixing the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll check in soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s on the right side, near my belly and lower abdomen. It started about four days ago and hurts more when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is it constant or does it come and go? And how would you rate the pain, on a scale from 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was an 8 at first, but now it’s around a 5. Lying still helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. You mentioned nausea too. Has that gotten worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s about the same. I still take Zofran in the morning like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had gastric bypass and now rely on tube feeds, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. After the surgery, I couldn’t keep food down, so I’ve been on tube feeds for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped your tube feeds for now and started IV fluids to let your gut rest. We also ordered a CT scan to check for any blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance something’s blocked? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your symptoms could also be from irritation or bacterial overgrowth. The CT will help us rule out a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my G-tube is still working fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is in place and the site looks clean. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. Good news — no signs of a blockage in your intestines. The G-tube is where it should be, in the excluded stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s likely due to irritation from the tube feeds or possibly bacterial overgrowth, which you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on rifaximin for that. Should we keep it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your rifaximin. We’ll also start adding back your tube feeds slowly tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but what if the pain comes back when we restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start very low and go slow. If you have any issues, we’ll pause and reassess. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better, maybe a 3 now. I slept okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to start your tube feeds again at a low rate — 20 cc per hour — and increase slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your morning Zofran. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your tube feeds at 20 cc/hr. The nurse will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little full, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enteral nutrition team just confirmed your feeds are infusing well at 20 cc/hr. No issues so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can we go higher later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll assess this afternoon. We don’t want to rush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back — all stable. White count is normal, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver and kidneys? I’ve had fatty liver before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Liver enzymes are normal. Kidney function is excellent. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is down to a 2. Feels like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ve increased your tube feeds to 40 cc/hr and plan to go to 60 by tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s my usual rate. I hope I can stay on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re optimistic. We’re also adding sucralfate to protect your stomach lining and lansoprazole for acid control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my past ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s preventive. We also added docusate for constipation, which can happen with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on 60 cc/hr for a few hours and tolerating it well. We’re calling that a success.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and you’re stable on full feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with wound care, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home health will visit to help with dressing changes. We’ll set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today. Pain is well-controlled, and you’re on full tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rifaximin twice daily, sucralfate three times a day, lansoprazole twice daily, docusate twice daily, and Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when should I call or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have a fever over 101.5, severe pain, vomiting, or redness around the tube site, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll follow up with your surgeon for an appointment. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — home health is set for wound care, and your pharmacy has your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I got the call. Everything’s arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — make sure to crush all pills before giving them through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember from last time. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And avoid heavy lifting for now. Let the incision heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Home health will visit tomorrow. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say I made it home safely. Everything’s set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful to hear. We’ll check in soon. Rest and recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling dizzy and nauseous. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been feeling lightheaded, especially when I stand up. It started about a week ago. I also feel dehydrated and nauseous, but I haven’t actually vomited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any other symptoms? Chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some palpitations, but no chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how’s your tube feeding been going? Are you tolerating it well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been okay, but I haven’t been drinking much water. I’ve been relying mostly on the tube feeds. I’ve also had some diarrhea the last couple of days, which is unusual for me—I’m usually constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. We’ll check your labs and start you on IV fluids to help with the dehydration. That should also help with the dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I was worried it might be my blood sugar again. I’ve had low sugars before when I don’t eat enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your glucose in the ER—it was 103, which is normal. But we’ll keep an eye on it, especially given your history of hypoglycemia after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. And my incision—when I wretch, it hurts a little there. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The exam shows your wound is healing well—red granulation tissue, no infection. A little discomfort with straining is expected. We’ll make sure it stays clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was also told I might have bacterial overgrowth before. Could that be acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. You’re already on rifaximin, which helps with that. We’ll continue it and see if symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my anxiety—sometimes I feel like my heart races, and I get lightheaded. Could that be part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Anxiety can definitely cause palpitations and dizziness. But we’ve ruled out serious heart issues—the ECG was normal, and your rhythm is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. So, what’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids for a few hours to rehydrate you. We’ll repeat some labs to make sure your electrolytes are balanced. Then, if you’re tolerating water, we’ll discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If things go well, yes. We just want to make sure you’re stable and symptoms are resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat labs look good—kidney function, electrolytes, and glucose are all stable. The IV fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I do feel a bit better. Less dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
