conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good you’re staying on track with meds. We’ll keep your tube feeds going but switch you to a different formula called Vivonex for now—it’s easier to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should. We also want to make sure there’s no infection or ulcer complication. Since you had an endoscopy recently, we won’t repeat it now, but we did order a CT scan to check your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the scan with contrast? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It helps us see if there’s any fluid, infection, or changes near your surgical sites. We’ll do it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. The pain is pretty strong—can I get something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. I’m going to order IV morphine for now, and we’ll adjust as needed. We also have Zofran for nausea if that comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I was really worried this might be another ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s definitely a concern given your history, but we’re monitoring closely. Your vital signs are stable, and you’re not running a fever, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back last night. Good news—it shows no abscess or phlegmon. The incision is healing, and there’s no new internal issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely related to your previous ulcer site or bowel motility. You mentioned bloating—sometimes slow movement in the intestines can cause discomfort like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could constipation be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re going to give you a Fleet’s enema to help move things along. If that works, it might relieve both the bloating and the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m willing to try anything that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I see you had a good bowel movement after the enema. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better, actually. The bloating is gone, and the pain has eased a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We also started your tube feeds with Vivonex this morning, and you’re tolerating it well. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the special formula you mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s designed for people with digestive issues after surgery. It’s low residue and easier on your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Should I keep using it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that at discharge. For now, we’re focused on keeping you comfortable and ensuring you’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or anemia. We’re going to switch your pain control from IV morphine to oral Dilaudid and Tylenol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. You’re afebrile, eating well through the tube, and your pain is much improved. That’s all positive progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been walking a little each day like they suggested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Staying mobile helps prevent complications and supports recovery. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things continue this way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the tube feeds, take sucralfate four times a day, and stay on your PPI. We’ll also keep you on rifaximin for bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember sucralfate coats the ulcer. Should I take it on an empty stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. One hour before feeds or two hours after. It works best when the stomach is empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the Dilaudid as needed, but call us if it doesn’t improve within a few hours or if you develop fever, vomiting, or dark stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’ve reviewed everything, and you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest, continue walking, stay hydrated. Avoid heavy lifting—nothing over 10 pounds—until your follow-up with surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health meds—I should keep taking those too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. Continue fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and clonazepam as prescribed. Your mental health is part of your overall recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scan or test soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless symptoms return. Focus on healing and following up with your surgeons and GI doctor as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, remember to apply mupirocin to your G-tube site twice daily to prevent infection, especially since you’ve had MRSA before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I almost forgot about that. I’ll start again today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep an eye on the site—let your doctor know if you see redness, swelling, or increased drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we’ll schedule your follow-up. In the meantime, get plenty of rest and keep up with your fluids and feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to focus on healing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re confident you’ll continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted last night with worsening abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. The pain started again in my upper belly, right under the ribs, and it’s spreading to the right side. It’s a burning feeling, worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned this has happened a few times recently. Are you having nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been nauseous and dry heaving. I haven’t eaten much the last day. I’m still doing tube feeds, but they don’t seem to bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers, chills, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. I had one loose stool yesterday, but this morning it was normal. I’m worried it might be another ulcer or maybe a stitch left behind from surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did you see anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows no abscess, infection, or blockage. Your gallbladder, liver, and pancreas look normal. The gastrostomy tube is in the right place. No signs of a new ulcer or perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear cause yet. But your pain could be related to inflammation or nerve sensitivity near the surgical site. Your labs are mostly normal—no infection or organ issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking acetaminophen at home, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on oxycodone every four hours for better pain control. We also want to increase your free water flushes through the tube to 100 mL every four hours. Dehydration can make pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing 60 mL three times a day. Is more water safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and should help keep you hydrated. We’ll monitor your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about long-term? I can’t keep coming back every few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re starting gabapentin, which helps with nerve-related pain. It may take a few days to work. You’ll follow up with the pain clinic after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin? I’ve heard of that. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We checked for interactions. We’re keeping all your usual meds—sucralfate, PPI, rifaximin, and your fluoxetine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also noticed a little leaking around my G-tube site. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked this morning. No redness or infection. A small amount of leakage can happen. Just keep the area clean and dry. Use the mupirocin ointment as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. The pain is still there, but not as sharp. The new meds might be helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We gave you a nutritional supplement through the tube yesterday to make sure you’re getting enough calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel any discomfort from it. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s well tolerated. Your labs this morning are looking good—white blood cell count is normal, and no signs of dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure your pain is stable on oral meds and you’re tolerating your regular tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications, including the new gabapentin three times a day and oxycodone every six hours as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need a prescription for those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get a six-week supply. Also, keep doing 100 mL water flushes every four hours. Watch for fever, vomiting, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the oxycodone first. If it doesn’t help within a few hours, or if you develop new symptoms, come back or call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-up with my surgeon and primary care. Should I mention the gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’re scheduled with the pain clinic next week. They may adjust the dose if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid any foods or activities?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No specific food restrictions. Just continue your regular tube feeding formula. Avoid heavy lifting for now, and listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your prescriptions and discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's been really bad for about a week. It's all over my belly, not just one spot. I feel bloated and crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nausea, and I threw up once—clear fluid—after I got here. No fever at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see your gastrostomy tube was changed five days ago because of leakage. Has the pain gotten worse since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been getting worse. I’m having loose stools a few times a day, but no blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—so your stomach can rest. We’ll give fluids through your IV and continue your tube feedings slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I stop my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll keep giving your usual medications through the tube, but we’ll crush the pills first. Some of your meds are important for your mood and stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve been using Tylenol for pain, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you something stronger for now. But first, we need to rule out serious causes. You’ve already had an X-ray, and it didn’t show a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just some normal gas patterns—nothing concerning like a bowel obstruction. But we’re going to do a CT scan tomorrow with contrast to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be safe with my bypass surgery history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We do these often in patients with gastric bypass. It will help us check for internal hernias or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. Good news—it shows no blockage, no hernia, and your gastrostomy tube is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see a clear structural cause. Given your history, it could be related to gut motility, irritation from the tube, or bacterial overgrowth. Your labs are stable—no infection or anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bacterial overgrowth before. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. You’re already on rifaximin, which helps with that. We’ll keep you on it and see if symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? What about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on oral pain meds—oxycodone liquid—and see how you do. Once you’re tolerating that, we can advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I stay on the IV fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper them as you tolerate tube feedings and oral intake. Right now, you’re on a stage 3 diet—blended foods—through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. The new pain med helped. I haven’t needed much nausea medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep monitoring. Try to walk a little each day—it helps your gut move and prevents clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been getting up. Is the heparin shot for blood clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We give it to all patients after surgery or with limited mobility. You’re also wearing compression boots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain is still improving, and you’re tolerating feedings well. We’re thinking you might go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on the stage 3 diet for now. No straws or gum—can increase gas. Keep crushing your pills and taking your meds, including the new sucralfate for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sucralfate? What does that do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It coats your stomach and any ulcers to help them heal. You’ll take it four times a day on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxycodone liquid as needed, every six hours. But avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers in your bypass anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—Tylenol is safer. What about activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can walk and do light activity, but no heavy lifting—nothing over 10 pounds—for six weeks. No abdominal exercises yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tube site? It was leaking before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it clean and dry. Use the mupirocin ointment twice a day to prevent infection. Showering is okay, but no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Vital signs are stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating and moving fine. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. When should I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your surgeon in one to two weeks. Call sooner if you develop fever, severe pain, vomiting, or trouble with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your gastric bypass reversal surgery. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a little nervous, but okay. I’ve been having those low blood sugar episodes a lot lately, even when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s what we’re hoping to fix with this reversal. The bypass has been causing your body to absorb food too quickly, leading to hypoglycemia. We’ll reconnect your stomach and intestines to slow things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve had this for years, and nothing else helped. The specialists said reversal was my best option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve reviewed your history, including your past ulcers and bacterial overgrowth. The plan is laparoscopic reversal, but we may convert to open if needed. Any questions before we proceed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need the G-tube after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. It’s there to help with stomach decompression after surgery. We’ll clamp it in a few days once your bowels start moving again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And pain control? Last time I had surgery, it was rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with an epidural for the first day or two, then switch to a PCA pump. Once you’re eating, we’ll move to oral pain meds like hydromorphone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, that sounds better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The anesthesia team will be in soon. We’ll see you after the surgery in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re in the recovery unit. The surgery went well—laparoscopic bypass reversal completed without complications. You were extubated and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I feel groggy, but okay. My stomach feels… different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will take time to adjust. We’ve reconnected your stomach to the jejunum, so digestion will be more normal. You’re NPO for now—G-tube is on gravity drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the staples? I see bandages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small incisions were stapled closed. They’ll heal in a few weeks. We’ll monitor for infection, but you’re on antibiotics and heparin to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood sugar? Should I check it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it every four hours. Your last was 111—normal. With the reversal, we expect fewer hypoglycemic episodes long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We did an upper GI study this morning with contrast. No leaks or blockages—great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I start drinking water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until tomorrow. For now, just keep using your mouth swabs. We want to make sure your stomach is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My pain is better—still there, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the epidural going today, then transition to oral meds soon. We’re also encouraging you to sit up and walk later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I don’t want to get a blood clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Early movement helps prevent that. You’re also wearing compression boots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look good. Hemoglobin is stable, no signs of bleeding. We’re going to clamp the G-tube today and start small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! Can I have more than a sip?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow—just a few sips every 15 minutes. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? I felt a little shaky earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it—123, which is fine. Sometimes the body reacts to stress. Keep monitoring, and let us know if you feel dizzy or sweaty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. You tolerated water, so we’re advancing you to clear liquids—broth, apple juice, gelatin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have juice? I’ve been craving something sweet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but small amounts. And remember, no straws or gum—those can cause bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the pain meds? I’m on hydromorphone now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oral hydromorphone as needed. We stopped the epidural yesterday. How’s the pain on a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4. Much better than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep it controlled. You’re also walking more—great for recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re advancing your diet to stage III—soft, pureed foods. Things like mashed potatoes, applesauce, yogurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have scrambled eggs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If they’re well-cooked and soft, yes. Small portions. We don’t want to overwhelm your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vitamins? I usually take them crushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue crushing all pills. We’ll also start you on chewable multivitamins to prevent deficiencies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Ate all your meals, walking independently, pain controlled. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the stage III diet until your follow-up. No straws, no gum. Monitor your blood sugar closely with your CGM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the glucose gel we’re prescribing. One packet, wait 15 minutes. If still low, repeat. If you pass out, call 911.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hydromorphone for breakthrough pain and acetaminophen for mild discomfort. Don’t drive while on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs are normal. No infection, no anemia. You’re afebrile and stable. Looks like we’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But what about the staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll be removed at your follow-up. Keep the area dry—showering is okay, no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I see drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Clear drainage is normal. Cover with gauze. But if it’s yellow, green, or foul-smelling, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day! You’ve passed all milestones. Tolerating diet, ambulating, no complications. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so relieved. What about my other meds—like fluoxetine and aripiprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home medications, but crush them. We’re also adding pantoprazole twice daily for a month to prevent reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no NSAIDs, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. No ibuprofen or naproxen. They can cause ulcers. Use acetaminophen instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re doing excellent—eating well, pain controlled, no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Just want to make sure I understand everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. No heavy lifting over 10 pounds for six weeks. Light exercise is fine, but no abdominal crunches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In two weeks. We’ll remove staples, check healing, and review your progress. Call sooner if you have fever, severe pain, or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Vital signs are stable, you’ve eaten breakfast, and your incisions look clean. All set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I feel like this surgery was the right choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful it will resolve your hypoglycemia. Keep monitoring, take your meds, and follow the diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling nauseous and not able to keep much down. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I started feeling nauseous two days ago. I’ve been trying to drink water and have some protein shakes, but they just come back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Have you vomited? And if so, what did it look like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I threw up twice this morning. It was greenish—kind of bile-colored. No blood, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. You mentioned you’ve been trying to hydrate—how much have you actually been able to keep down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not much. Two instant breakfast drinks, a cup of broth, and just sips of water yesterday. I feel dizzy when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That dizziness could be from dehydration. We’ll start you on IV fluids right away to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been taking Zofran for the nausea, but it hasn’t helped much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll adjust your anti-nausea medication. You’re already on Ondansetron—Zofran—but we can add another one that works differently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Would that be safe with my other meds? I take a lot since the bypass reversal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll check for interactions. You’re on Lansoprazole, Sucralfate, Rifaximin—those are all for stomach protection and bacterial balance, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. And I’ve been on a Stage 3 bariatric diet since the surgery. I thought I was doing okay until this hit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes protein shakes can be harder to tolerate after surgery. We’ll switch you to a mechanical soft diet—things like broth, cream of wheat—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds easier. Should I stop the protein shakes completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll reintroduce them slowly once the nausea settles. We don’t want to overwhelm your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any idea what’s causing this? I was doing so well after the reversal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a temporary issue with digestion adjusting. We’ll monitor you, make sure there’s no infection or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a stool test today, right? Was anything found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked for infections like Salmonella, Shigella, C. diff, and parasites. All came back negative, which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection, and your labs show your electrolytes are stable. Kidney function is good too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? I’ve been a bit anemic in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is a little low at 10.8, but it hasn’t dropped. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no need for transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my G-tube—is that still okay? It’s capped, but I want to make sure it’s not leaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—the tube is secure, no leakage. The incision site looks clean, no redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about infections, especially with my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. You’re on mupirocin for MRSA colonization, which helps reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some broth and cream of wheat last night and kept it down. No vomiting since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep you on the mechanical soft diet and continue the IV fluids until you’re consistently tolerating oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start walking more? I’ve been up a little, but I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. Ambulating helps your digestion and prevents blood clots. Just take it slow—we want you moving, not straining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? It’s been mild, just using Tylenol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s perfect. You can keep using Tylenol as needed. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—no NSAIDs. I’ll stick to Tylenol and the liquid pain med if I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. We’re going to discharge you this morning. You’re tolerating food, hydrated, and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the mechanical soft diet—no straws, no gum. We’re adding Compazine for nausea—you can alternate it with Zofran if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Should I crush them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, crush all pills to avoid irritation. And no heavy lifting for six weeks. Moderate exercise is fine, but no abdominal strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the G-tube site? Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can shower. If there’s any clear drainage, cover it with clean gauze. Call us if you see redness, swelling, or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the nausea comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the Compazine first. If you can’t keep anything down for 12 hours, or if you develop a fever over 101.5, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your follow-up—we’ll see you soon to check your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago—just a dull ache at first, but it got worse yesterday. Now it's sharp in the middle and upper part of my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I threw up once this morning. It was dark, but I don’t think it was blood. I haven’t eaten anything since the pain started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your history shows you’ve had similar pain before and a few G-tube placements. Are you still on tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m off the 24-hour feeds now. I’ve been on a bariatric stage 3 diet—soft foods. But I stopped everything when the pain came on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. We’ll start IV fluids and manage your pain. We also need to check your G-tube site and get a CT scan to see what’s going on near the surgical area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the pain get worse? I’m worried it’s another leak or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for that. The CT will help us rule out a leak. For now, we’ll give you IV pain meds and keep your G-tube to gravity drainage—that often helps relieve pressure and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT results back. There’s significant inflammation near the spot where your stomach was reconnected after the bypass reversal. No clear leak, but we can’t rule out a tiny one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it infected? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like inflammation, possibly from irritation or early infection. We’re starting you on antibiotics—ciprofloxacin and metronidazole—to cover any possible infection. We’ll keep you NPO a bit longer and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on IV meds the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. But if you improve, we’ll switch to oral meds and slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still some discomfort, but not as sharp. The nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to clamp your G-tube today and see how you tolerate it. If all goes well, we’ll start a very light diet—bariatric stage 4—later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s in stage 4? I don’t want to set myself back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s pureed foods—smooth, no chunks. We’ll start small and watch for cramping or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to stop the diet advancement. You had some cramping after the stage 4 meal, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it came back—mild but uncomfortable. I think my stomach just can’t handle food yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. We’re going back to NPO and keeping the G-tube to gravity. Also, your tube has been leaking—probably due to a small hole. We’ve scheduled an exchange for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a surgery? I’m nervous about another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not surgery. Interventional radiology will do it under fluoroscopy—using X-ray guidance. You’ll get light sedation. It’s routine and low risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. Will I be able to eat after they change it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO overnight after the exchange, then reassess. If all looks good, we’ll try advancing your diet again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you just got back from the G-tube exchange. It went smoothly—new 18 French MIC tube is in place and working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much—just some pressure. Is it safe to start eating now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO tonight as a precaution. Tomorrow, we’ll start with stage 5—almost regular soft foods—and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you tolerated the stage 5 diet well. No pain, no nausea. Your urine output is good, and you’re walking without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We’ll switch your pain meds to oral—acetaminophen and a small amount of oxycodone if needed. You’ll finish a 10-day course of antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on the soft diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the bariatric stage 5 diet. Avoid tough or fibrous foods. And crush all pills—no tablets whole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds—like Zofran and gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home medications unless we told you otherwise. We’re adding docusate for constipation prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube? How do I care for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the site clean and dry. Check daily for redness or drainage. The tube can stay clamped unless you're using it for feeds. We’ll follow up with your surgeon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever, vomiting, severe pain, dark stools, or signs of dehydration—like dizziness or dry mouth—call us or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no driving with the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Avoid driving or heavy machinery while on oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take ciprofloxacin twice daily and metronidazole three times daily for 10 days. Finish the whole course, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And follow up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in about a week. They’ll check your G-tube and assess your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—any new pain or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling good. Just ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Nurse will go over your meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’ll follow up and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Rest, stay hydrated, and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I worry about this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The inflammation was likely due to irritation near the surgical site. With the antibiotics and proper diet, it should resolve. But yes, given your history, we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing everything right. Just keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.text: I packed up. Just waiting on the discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having trouble keeping food down and have some pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back mostly normal—no signs of infection or pancreatitis. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. You’re scheduled for an upper GI study today with contrast to check for any blockages, leaks, or ulcers.

conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’m a little anxious about it.

conversation_lines.text: It’s not painful. You’ll drink a liquid that shows up on X-ray, and we’ll watch how it moves. It helps us see what’s going on inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The upper GI is back—good news. No leaks, no blockages, and no strictures. Your anatomy looks intact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still in pain and nauseous?

conversation_lines.text: I was on Vivonex before. Can we try that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having a burning pain in your chest and upper belly for the past few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad—like a fire moving up from my stomach into my throat. It feels just like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you didn’t stop your tube feeds before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I kept them going. I only drank water by mouth. I didn’t want to make things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had this kind of pain before, linked to reflux and ulcers after your gastric bypass reversal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. Last time, changing the feeding formula and starting erythromycin helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started you on an IV medication—pantoprazole—to reduce stomach acid and protect your esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Is it safe to keep my tube feeds going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing them. We’re also increasing the rate a bit because your nutrition needs are high. We want to avoid another drop in your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about that too. The hypoglycemia scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. Your erythromycin is still running—it helps your stomach empty better, which should help with both reflux and sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cholestyramine? I’ve never taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It binds bile acids that can worsen reflux. It’s often helpful in cases like yours. We’ll give it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. Should I be worried about the pain getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. We did an X-ray earlier—no blockage or free air. Your bowels look normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Do you think it’s another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. The GI team wants to do an EGD—upper endoscopy—to check your stomach and the surgical connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll keep you comfortable until then. We also added prochlorperazine for nausea if it flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want this burning to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well during the EGD this morning. I have the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? Did you see what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. There’s inflammation in your stomach—gastritis—and some small, healing ulcers near the surgical connection where your stomach meets the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not bleeding or perforated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the ulcers are clean-based, which means they’re not actively bleeding. There’s also a slight narrowing in your stomach anatomy that may be slowing emptying and contributing to reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why the burning keeps coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The GI team recommends staying on the pantoprazole, but now twice a day instead of once. We’ll also keep the sucralfate to coat the ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing it. It helps move things through. We’re also adding ranitidine at bedtime—it gives extra acid control overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I try eating anything by mouth now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips and soft foods. Your stomach needs time to heal. If you tolerate it, we’ll gradually increase.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is much better, and you’ve kept down your oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the burning is mostly gone. I had some applesauce and broth yesterday with no problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to reduce your tube feeds back to your home rate since you’re eating more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I prefer to eat normally when I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep supporting you. Your labs are stable—no anemia worsening, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made steady progress. Pain is controlled, you’re tolerating a full stage 3 diet, and your bowel function is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on Friday. We’ll make sure you have all your medications sorted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need new prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll take pantoprazole twice daily now, cholestyramine twice a day, and ranitidine at night. All your other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual schedule—continuous overnight and bolus during the day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up is set with Dr. Kim next week. They’ll monitor your ulcer healing and reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Should I sleep upright?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, elevate the head of your bed. It helps reduce nighttime reflux. Also avoid lying down right after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re pain-free, eating well, and labs are stable. Discharge is tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: call if the pain returns, or if you vomit blood, run a fever, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking all the meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your tube site looks great—no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep resting, stay upright after meals, and follow up with Dr. Kim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, thank you. I’ve been worried about another ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work came back—white count is normal, no signs of infection or bleeding. That supports this being inflammation, not something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rifaximin? I’ve been on that for bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep that too. It’s not related to the pain flare, but it’s important for your gut balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? Has the medication helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some discomfort, but not sharp or constant like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring and adjust as needed. We’re planning to place a PICC line tomorrow so you can go home on IV pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And how long will I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your tube feeds are running well, and you’re not vomiting—that’s a positive sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be awake during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in place. We did a chest X-ray, and it’s positioned correctly in the large vein near your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to feel well and your pain stays controlled on oral meds, we’ll discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set—you’re cleared to go home. You’ll take pantoprazole through the PICC twice a day, and a nurse will visit to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your meds, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: So if it’s not a clot or infection, why does my arm hurt so much?

conversation_lines.text: Are you saying we should take it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since you’re able to eat a soft bariatric diet now and your tube feeds are going well, we can switch back to oral pantoprazole. That means we can remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help my stomach pain?

conversation_lines.text: We hope so. The oral medication should still control the acid. We’ll monitor you tonight, and if your pain is stable and you keep tolerating food, we can discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the arm pain? Will that go away after removing the PICC?

conversation_lines.text: It might not go away completely right now. This is likely a long-term issue we’ll manage over time. The goal is to find a balance—meds, diet, and tube feeds—that lets you feel better and live well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll still need the G-tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue tube feeds at 50 mL/hr with Jevity 1.5. Your home formula will need to be updated—your outpatient team will help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds? How long do I take them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Erythromycin for 7 days, rifaximin for 7 days. But don’t stop them—discuss continuing at your follow-up with bariatric surgery. We’ve confirmed rifaximin is covered by your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing tube feeds, drink water or Ensure shakes, and slowly add soft foods as tolerated. Avoid heavy meals. Take all your meds, including the new ones. Call if pain worsens or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See bariatric surgery soon. They’ll review the H. pylori result and decide next steps. We’ll send them a full summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m nervous, but I feel like we have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do. We’re here to support you. Take it one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Keep using the tube, take the meds, go slow with food, and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing—should I be worried about the pain never going away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may not disappear completely, but we can manage it. It’ll take time and teamwork with your providers. The goal is improvement, not perfection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thanks for being honest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re in this together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. You’ll go home in the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand the meds, feeds, and follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Erythromycin and rifaximin for a week, pantoprazole, sucralfate, tube feeds at 50 mL/hr, and see bariatric surgery soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll call you in a few days to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Let us know how you’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for seeing me. I was just discharged three days ago, but yesterday the pain around my G-tube got a lot worse. It’s different—more focused there, not all over like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was there any injury? Did you lift something or fall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was just walking around. No heavy lifting or falls. I thought maybe taking a night off from tube feeds would help, but it didn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. I’ve been keeping down clear liquids—Ensure and Carnation breakfast drink. Last bowel movement was yesterday, normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Let me examine you quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube looks okay—no redness or signs of infection. But I notice tenderness right around the site, especially when you tense your abdomen. That’s called Carnett’s sign, which suggests the pain might be from the abdominal wall muscles, not inside the belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s not the tube itself or an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. We also did an X-ray called a KUB. It shows no blockage or free air, which is reassuring. But there is some gaseous distention in the stomach area, possibly from your prior gastric bypass anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be making the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the main focus now seems to be the abdominal wall. We’ll hold your tube feeds overnight to rest your gut and restart them tomorrow if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been using the oxycodone, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re going to adjust your pain meds. We’ll increase your gabapentin from 300 mg to 600 mg three times a day. It works better for nerve or musculoskeletal pain like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. Should help. What about the erythromycin and rifaximin I started last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue both. They’re for bacterial overgrowth, which you’ve had before. We’ll finish a 14-day course to make sure it’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve been worried this pain means something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But right now, everything looks stable. No signs of infection or obstruction. We’ll keep monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been feeling anxious about it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for you to meet with a social worker today. They can help with coping strategies and connect you with your outpatient therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? Any change since we adjusted the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less sharp. I’m not in distress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’ll keep an eye on it overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We checked your labs this morning. Your white blood cell count is a bit low—2.8—but it’s improved from yesterday and not due to infection. We’ll repeat it in a week as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level, especially since you’re not sick. It’s slightly below your baseline, but no medication or infection seems to be causing it. Just a quick check in a week to make sure it stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart your tube feeds at the goal rate—50 mL/hr of Jevity 1.5. Nutrition recommends this formula for better tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using Jevity 1.2. Is the change okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. But you’ll need your outpatient provider to prescribe it. Let your GI doctor know when you follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain been since restarting feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No worse. Actually, feels about like my usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. And your G-tube site? Any redness or warmth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little redness, but it’s not getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse noted minimal erythema, but it’s improving. We’ll keep the mupirocin ointment on it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if things stay on track. Pain is at baseline, you’re tolerating feeds, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I call my GI doctor soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Continue working with them on your chronic pain. We’ve updated your meds—higher gabapentin, same antidepressants and acid reducers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your pain is stable, you’re moving well, and labs are okay. Remember: finish the erythromycin and rifaximin, keep the CBC follow-up, and talk to your GI doctor about any new concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better knowing it’s not something dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain for the past three days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started while I was visiting my son. It’s sharp and right around my feeding tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the pain constant? Does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s constant and sharp. It gets worse when I eat solids or when the tube feeds are running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve had no fever, vomiting, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been passing gas and having normal bowel movements. No redness or drainage at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history, we’ll start with some blood work and a chest X-ray to rule out infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stop my tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold them for now to see if that helps your pain. But we’ll give you IV fluids with dextrose to prevent low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I do get shaky if my sugar drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back normal—no signs of infection or organ issues. The chest X-ray was clear too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It seems related to your tube site and possibly your stomach lining. We’ll keep you NPO for now and continue IV dextrose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need to stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess in a day or two. If your pain improves, we’ll try small oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain seems a bit better today. We’re going to start weaning off the IV dextrose slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try eating something small?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with sips of water and light snacks. We’ll monitor your blood sugar every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. I’m worried I won’t get enough calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tracking your intake. If it’s too low, we may add a medication to help with appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars are stable in the low 100s. But your oral intake is still below target—about 60% of your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just not very hungry. Everything feels full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start Marinol, a medication that can help stimulate your appetite. It’s often used in cases like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like medical marijuana?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a synthetic form that helps with appetite without strong psychoactive effects. We’ll start low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your intake improved yesterday. You hit about 85% of your calorie goal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit hungrier. Is that the Marinol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely so. We’ll keep it going. We’re also arranging a dietitian consult to help plan your meals after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be helpful. I always worry about my sugar dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you specific instructions on small, frequent meals with protein and low-glycemic carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been pain-free for two days now. We’re going to restart your tube feeds at a low rate to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that bring the pain back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slowly. If pain returns, we’ll stop again. But the goal is to see if you can eventually stop the tube altogether.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I could stop the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the long-term plan—over several months. If you can maintain nutrition by mouth and stay pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the low-rate tube feeds well overnight. No pain or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t feel anything. That’s a good sign, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’ll continue to increase the rate gradually and monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The dietitian met with you yesterday. How did that go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really helpful. She gave me a meal plan and tips for snacking safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ll follow up with her as an outpatient too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge for early next week. You’re doing well—pain-free and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I still need the tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. But we’ll follow up in a few weeks to reassess. The goal is to remove it eventually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work is stable, and you’ve maintained over 90% of your calorie needs orally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sticking to the dietitian’s plan. I feel more in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want to hear. We’ll keep your pain meds and stomach medications the same for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling your follow-up with Dr. Patel in four weeks. They’ll help monitor your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dietitian too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll see them first. They’ll adjust your plan based on how you’re doing.
