conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more day and we’ll discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But what if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us. We’ll want to know. But keep taking your medications and stick to the diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. You’re afebrile, pain-free, and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood sugar monitoring?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check it before meals and at bedtime. And wear the Dexcom monitor we discussed to track trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And take my meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll see you in follow-up, and we’ll decide then about the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick visit—we’re documenting that you received your final tube feeding before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It went fine. No pain at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Keep up the great work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Call if anything changes. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I woke up this morning with sharp pain near my G-tube, and it’s been constant. It goes around to my left side. Every time I tried to eat, I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or diarrhea. Just the pain and vomiting with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of gastric bypass reversal and previous ulcers, we’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food at all? What about my tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold the tube feeds for now too. We’ll give you IV fluids to keep you hydrated and prevent low blood sugar, which we know you’re at risk for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had this before—last time they helped me with Marinol for appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart Marinol. We’ll also give you Zofran and Compazine for nausea. And we’ll vent your G-tube to relieve any pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just hope it’s not another long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it day by day. Your labs look normal so far—no signs of infection or pancreatitis. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work from last night is stable—normal white count, liver enzymes, lipase, and glucose. We’re going to keep you NPO today and recheck how you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. The nausea is better since the Zofran. The pain is still there but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep managing the pain and nausea. We’re planning a CT scan today with contrast to make sure there’s no leak or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a CT a few months ago that showed inflammation near the anastomosis. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s possible. But that scan didn’t show a leak. We’ll compare today’s to see if anything’s changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT came back. Good news—no signs of abscess, obstruction, or leak. The anastomosis looks normal, and your G-tube is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a clear answer yet. It could be related to inflammation or irritation from the tube. Since you’re not vomiting and labs are stable, we’ll try advancing your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m willing to try. But slowly, please.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to start you on clear liquids. Small sips. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to full liquids later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ve been craving something to drink. Will I still get the Marinol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. And we’ll keep your PPI and sucralfate to protect your stomach lining, especially since your last endoscopy showed ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had a few sips of apple juice and some broth. No nausea or pain so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll advance you to full liquids—yogurt, pudding, maybe some protein shakes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a small meal later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s take it slow. We want to make sure you don’t relapse. Your blood sugar has been stable—staying in the 100s—which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well yesterday. Today, we’ll try a soft, low-fat, low-sugar meal. Small portions. And we’ll clamp your G-tube to see how you do without venting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still avoid tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. Since you’re tolerating food, we’ll focus on oral intake. That’s actually the goal—getting you off tube feeds if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I ate half a scrambled egg and some toast. Felt fine. No pain, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fantastic. The nutritionist reviewed your intake and said you’re meeting over 75% of your calorie needs. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the Dexcom like they told me. My sugars are staying steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s exactly what we want. You’re managing your hypoglycemia well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ve done really well—no pain, no vomiting, good oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your home meds: fluoxetine, aripiprazole, gabapentin, atorvastatin, and the PPI. Also, sucralfate four times a day, Marinol twice a day, and Zofran as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a small amount of liquid oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but use it sparingly. Acetaminophen is safer for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I restart tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. Focus on small, frequent meals—low glycemic carbs, high protein. The dietitian will help you fine-tune this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a follow-up with her next week. Should I wear the Dexcom all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. It helps catch lows before they become dangerous. Test your sugars before meals and at bedtime too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your surgeon. If it’s severe or you start vomiting, come back to the ER. But I think you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got your CT report back. Confirms no acute issues—no leak, no obstruction. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Sometimes the pain is from irritation or inflammation that doesn’t show up on scans. But you’ve responded well to conservative care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. We’ll send all your prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep up with your diet, meds, and follow-ups. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep the G-tube site clean and dry. Use the mupirocin ointment as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember from last time. I’ll take good care of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had terrible diarrhea for two days—more than nine times a day. I also started vomiting, eight times yesterday, and the last one had a little blood in it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any fever, chills, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or chills. No black or bloody stools. But my stomach pain near the G-tube is worse, and I haven’t eaten since the diarrhea started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were just discharged a week ago for similar pain, right? And you’re on oxycodone for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The pain is under control with the oxycodone, but only when I take it on schedule. Without it, it’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll make sure you get your pain meds on time. Now, you took loperamide—Imodium—for the diarrhea, and then the vomiting started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my bariatric surgeon suggested it, but right after I took it, I felt nauseous and started vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not uncommon. Sometimes slowing the gut down when there’s an infection can make nausea worse. We’ll hold off on Imodium for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But why the blood in the vomit? I’m worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that you vomited so many times, it’s likely from a small tear in the throat or stomach from the force—what we call a Mallory-Weiss tear. It’s usually minor and heals on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. No more vomiting since I got here, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll give you IV fluids to rehydrate you and start a medication to help with nausea—ondansetron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube? Should I be using it for feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and hold tube feeds until your diarrhea improves. We don’t want to stress your gut further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your electrolytes are a bit off—bicarb is low, which makes sense with all the vomiting—but nothing critical. Your kidney function and liver tests are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my blood sugar okay? I usually check it because of my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, glucose was 98, which is stable. No signs of hypoglycemia. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a simple X-ray—just to check your bowel gas pattern. No signs of obstruction or ileus. Everything looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about the stool test they took?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It came back positive for norovirus—specifically Norovirus GII. That explains the sudden vomiting and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, like the stomach flu? Is it contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very contagious. But we’re taking precautions. You’ll need to stay isolated for a few days, and your husband should wear gloves and wash hands well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure he knows. So it’s viral—no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Antibiotics won’t help and could make it worse. We’re treating it supportively—fluids, rest, and letting it run its course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. Only two episodes of diarrhea last night. Still nauseous, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll start you on a light bariatric diet—small sips of clear liquids, then advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a protein shake? I usually do well with those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start with broth and apple juice. If you tolerate that, we can try a small amount of protein later. We don’t want to rush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well this morning—no vomiting, and only one loose stool. Your electrolytes are improving too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I stop the IV now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for now, but we’re close. We’ll switch to oral meds and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had a good night—no diarrhea, no nausea. Labs this morning are normal. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your usual meds—pantoprazole, sucralfate, oxycodone for pain, and ondansetron if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dronabinol for appetite? I had a weird reaction last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on that for now. Your appetite should come back as you recover. We’ll discuss restarting it with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube? I’ve been thinking—maybe it’s time to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a conversation to have with your bariatric surgeon. Since you’re eating better, it might be possible. Follow up with them soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest at home, stay hydrated, and call if symptoms return. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea again—can you tell me how you’ve been feeling since you got home from the hospital three days ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not better, honestly. The nausea never went away. I tried to eat a little, but I just couldn’t keep anything down. The diarrhea’s still there too—watery, no blood. I was so weak I had to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any fever, chills, or new abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just the same dull pain I’ve had for years around my stomach and near the G-tube. Nothing worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs show your potassium is normal, but your AST and alkaline phosphatase are a bit high—probably from dehydration or your liver history. No signs of infection in your blood so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it still the norovirus? I thought that was supposed to go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. Sometimes it lasts longer in people with gastric surgery. We’re not repeating stool tests since you just had them. We’ll treat it as ongoing viral gastroenteritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids to rehydrate you, and we’ll keep giving you Zofran for nausea. We’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I use my G-tube for feeds? That’s how I got nutrition before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off on tube feeds for now. They might make the diarrhea worse while your gut is still inflamed. We’ll rely on your mouth for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my iron pill? I usually take it every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your iron for now—it can worsen nausea. You’ll restart it at home when you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain meds? I’ve been using the liquid oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using acetaminophen and gabapentin for now. We’re limiting opioids because they can slow the gut and make nausea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just don’t want the pain to flare up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If it gets bad, we’ll adjust. For now, rest and let your gut heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your white count is a bit low, but stable. Potassium dropped a little—3.7—so we’ll watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? The low white count?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It can happen with viral infections. We’re not seeing signs of bacterial infection, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I was able to sip some broth last night without throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll advance you to clear liquids today—apple juice, broth, maybe some Jell-O. Small sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try a soft food later, like mashed potatoes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s see how you do today. If no nausea or vomiting, we can try soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your stomach doing? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little queasy, but not bad. I had half a cup of apple juice an hour ago and it stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. I’ll order another dose of Zofran to keep that nausea in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m really hoping I can eat more soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. Your body just needs time to recover from the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are looking better. White count is up, potassium is 3.8—still a bit low but improving. You made it through the night without vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes! I had broth and crackers for dinner and a protein shake before bed. All stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fantastic. We’ll advance you to soft foods today—mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs, maybe some oatmeal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have toast? I miss real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, plain toast is fine. Just go slow—small bites, chew well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And can I restart my multivitamin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can restart your multivitamin and pantoprazole. But we’ll keep holding the iron for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the soft diet going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good! I ate mashed potatoes and chicken today. Only a little nausea after, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep you on softs tonight and try regular food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You tolerated soft foods well. We’re going to try a regular diet today—small portions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have a sandwich?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, turkey or chicken sandwich, no mayo. And keep drinking fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my G-tube—do I still need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. Since you’re eating better, the bariatric team recommends follow-up to discuss removing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. It’s been a hassle, and I don’t want it if I don’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. For now, keep the site clean. There’s a little crusting, but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’ve kept down regular meals, no vomiting, and your labs are stable. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What meds should I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds—pantoprazole, gabapentin, fluoxetine, atorvastatin. Restart your iron and multivitamin. And you’ll have Zofran and Compazine for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP in a week, and schedule with your bariatric surgeon about the G-tube removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like I’m finally turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard for it. Keep resting, eat small meals, and call if nausea or diarrhea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. A little tired, but no nausea. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your husband is here, and we’ll have you out within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. Continue all meds, follow up with your doctors, and focus on nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already feeling better. See you at follow-up!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The vomiting started last night, and the diarrhea began about three days ago. I’ve had pain around my G-tube site too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned your G-tube was recently changed and the balloon was upsized. Did the pain get worse after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Right after the change, the pain increased. And when I restarted tube feeds last weekend, the diarrhea started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You stopped the tube feeds when the symptoms got worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I stopped them the night before last. I just couldn’t keep anything down, even by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’ve had similar episodes before, including norovirus. Any blood in your vomit or stool this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no blood. Just clear vomit and loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ll start you on IV fluids to rehydrate you and keep you on bowel rest for now—no food or tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait and see how you do. Once the nausea settles, we’ll try clear liquids and go from there. We don’t want to rush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fair. My anxiety’s been worse with all this. It’s hard not knowing what’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve asked Psychiatry to see you to help manage the anxiety during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been on lorazepam and fluoxetine—should I keep taking those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your regular meds unless there’s a reason to adjust. We’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from yesterday show your white count was low at first but came up today—looks like no active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? No infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s reassuring. Your liver enzymes were slightly elevated but stable. Nothing suggests pancreatitis—lipase was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a little better overnight. Nausea’s not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll try advancing your diet today—start with clear liquids and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water and broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Small sips at first. We’ll monitor you closely. If no vomiting in a few hours, we’ll move to full liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well with clear liquids. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some apple juice and broth and didn’t vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll try a soft diet now—things like mashed potatoes and applesauce. Still no tube feeds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When might I be able to restart tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that before discharge. For now, let’s focus on oral intake. Your body needs time to settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the soft diet well yesterday. Today, we’ll try a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I’m hungry!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but start slow. We’ll bring a small meal. If you do well, you can have more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well with the regular diet. No nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. The diarrhea’s improved too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep you on your usual medications, including pantoprazole and sucralfate for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking ranitidine at night too. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that as well. It helps reduce stomach acid and may ease irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry saw you yesterday. They think your anxiety is contributing to your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it plays a role. They mentioned a clonidine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re not using it here because your blood pressure has been on the lower side—systolic in the 80s to 90s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ll talk to my outpatient psychiatrist about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. For now, we’ll keep using lorazepam as needed and continue your fluoxetine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been doing so well—eating normally, no vomiting, pain is controlled. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or come back if you start vomiting again, can’t keep fluids down, or have signs of dehydration—like dizziness or dry mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the G-tube? When can I restart feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend holding off for now. Follow up with your bariatric surgeon before restarting. They may want to assess the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve been using oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with a small prescription for oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but try to use it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to rely on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’re tolerating food, pain is mild, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like I can manage now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your regular meds—pantoprazole, sucralfate, ranitidine, and your psychiatric medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cholestyramine and bisacodyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those as prescribed. They help with bowel control and cholesterol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my doctors. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest for a few days, stay hydrated, and avoid heavy lifting until you see your surgeon. And no driving while on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send discharge instructions with all this. If anything changes, don’t hesitate to call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really appreciate all the care. I was so worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep in touch with your team, and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain started about two days ago. It’s in my upper right side, and I’ve been nauseous, throwing up a few times—nothing bloody. I also had loose stools for a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you haven’t been able to keep anything down, including your medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I couldn’t take anything. I’ve been so nauseous. I was worried it was my gallbladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan and an ultrasound of your right upper quadrant. Good news—no gallstones, no cholecystitis. Your liver looks fatty, which we already knew, but nothing acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging didn’t show any blockages, ulcers, or inflammation. Given your history of gastric bypass reversal and chronic pain, this might be a flare-up of your usual abdominal issues. We’ll keep monitoring and support you while we figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had pain before, but this one feels different—more in the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll keep that in mind. For now, you’re on IV fluids, and we’ll start you on your regular meds by mouth when you’re ready. We’ll also check labs to make sure nothing’s off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs came back—everything looks stable. Liver enzymes are slightly elevated but unchanged from before. No sign of infection or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try some food? I’m still nauseous but maybe a cracker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can start with clear liquids and see how you do. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance slowly. We also gave you ondansetron for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You made it through the night okay? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting, but the diarrhea stopped and now I haven’t had a bowel movement in two days. My stomach feels bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not uncommon. Sometimes when diarrhea stops and we give pain meds, things slow down. We’ll check an X-ray to see if there’s stool buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Full bowels can make you feel crampy and nauseous. We’ll start a gentle bowel regimen if the X-ray shows loading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The X-ray showed mild fecal loading, so we’ve started you on senna and docusate. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less sharp. I’m walking a bit more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Movement helps with both pain and bowel function. We’re also going to start gabapentin. It helps with nerve-related pain, which might be part of what you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. It made me sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start low and go slow. We want to help your pain without making you drowsy. And we’re not using opioids because they can worsen constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a bowel movement yesterday—great. How’s your nausea and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some ache, but not like before. I had toast this morning—no problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep advancing your diet. The gabapentin seems to be helping. We’ll increase it a bit today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been thinking—why do I keep having these episodes? Is something wrong with my stomach after the reversal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good question. Your recent endoscopy was normal—no ulcers or inflammation. The imaging is clear. So it’s not an infection or blockage. It may be that your nerves are extra sensitive after surgery, or your brain interprets gut signals differently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not ‘in my head’—but my nerves are just more reactive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s real pain, but it may not come from damage. That’s why we’re using gabapentin—it calms overactive nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain score down, eating regular food, moving around. We’ll keep the gabapentin going and the bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been gassy since starting the stool softeners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can add simethicone for gas. It’s over-the-counter and helps break up bubbles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray today showed improvement in stool loading. You’re making progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter. The gas is better with the simethicone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that on board. Your labs today are normal too. We’re thinking about discharge in a day or two if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We checked a stool test, but it was cancelled because the sample was too formed. But we did rule out Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t food poisoning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, looks like it wasn’t infectious. More likely a flare of your chronic condition, possibly triggered by stress or diet, but we can’t pinpoint it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if this happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally valid. We’ll send you home with a plan: gabapentin for nerve pain, stool softeners to prevent constipation, and simethicone for gas. Keep taking your regular meds like pantoprazole and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the gabapentin, stay hydrated, walk, and use the bowel regimen. If it gets severe or you can’t keep fluids down, come back. But you’ve handled this well—chances are you’ll do okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days with minimal pain, normal bowel movements, and no nausea. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Can I stop the gabapentin eventually?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend continuing it. You’ll follow up with chronic pain clinic—they may adjust the dose, but it’s helping your nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on so many pain meds over the years. I don’t want to get dependent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin isn’t addictive like opioids. It’s safe long-term. We’re avoiding opioids because they made the constipation worse and didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I felt foggy on them anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day. Your labs are normal, you’re walking, eating, and pain is mild. We’ll write your discharge orders this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your home meds. New ones: acetaminophen for pain, gabapentin three times a day, senna and docusate daily, miralax and bisacodyl as needed, and simethicone for gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No narcotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. They weren’t helping and were making constipation worse. The new plan focuses on nerve pain and bowel health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little anxious about managing this at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Your husband is listed as your contact—he can help. And your mental health is stable on your current meds. Keep in touch with your psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re discharged. Keep following the bowel and pain plan. Follow up with chronic pain, neurology, and your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Listen to your body, stay active, and don’t hesitate to reach out if things change. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I worry about my fatty liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something to monitor, but it’s not causing your pain. Keep up with your primary doctor on that. Diet and exercise help, but we know it’s complicated with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve made real progress this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I came in. I was scared it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. But it’s good we ruled out emergencies. Now it’s about managing the chronic part the best we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll start the gabapentin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Take it with food to avoid stomach upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the senna—I’ll take it every morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with docusate. It’s a gentle combo to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned a lot this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re here to support you. Call your doctors if you have questions. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Safe travels, and feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel better than I have in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best news. Keep building on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with the pain clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. They’ll help fine-tune your plan. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had this sharp pain in my upper belly, right in the middle, for about two days. It’s constant and burning. I also feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t thrown up or had a fever. No diarrhea either. But I haven’t been eating much because I feel full quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you’ve had similar pain before. You mentioned it might be gastritis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about a month ago. But my bariatric surgeon stopped my stomach meds—pantoprazole, Carafate, and ranitidine—and I haven’t been on them since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be important. Stopping those suddenly might have led to stomach irritation again. We’ll check that out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that really cause this much pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your history. After gastric bypass and reversal, your stomach is more sensitive. We’ll run some tests to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. White blood cell count, liver enzymes, and lipase are all normal. No sign of infection or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your CT scan showed no blockages, ulcers, or free fluid. Nothing structural causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and the timing after stopping stomach meds, this looks like a flare of gastritis—irritation of the stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So restarting those meds might help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re restarting pantoprazole, Carafate, and ranitidine. You’ll also get Tylenol for pain, since we want to avoid NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I’m allergic to those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your chart shows NSAID allergy. Tylenol is safe. We’ll also check your blood pressure—it was a bit low when you arrived.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood pressure sitting and standing. It drops a bit when you stand—orthostatic hypotension. That’s likely from not eating or drinking enough due to nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have been dizzy when I stand. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually, but it can increase fall risk. We’re giving you IV fluids to help, and it should improve as you start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still there, but not as sharp. The nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The meds are helping. We’ll keep encouraging small, frequent meals and nutritional supplements like Carnation Breakfast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying. But I get full so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after your surgeries. Nutrition will help guide you on high-calorie, nutrient-dense options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a cortisol level today because of the low blood pressure. It came back normal, so we don’t think it’s an adrenal issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What would that have meant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low cortisol could cause low blood pressure and fatigue, but it’s not the case here. Your symptoms are likely from poor intake and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs look stable. Hemoglobin is slightly lower but not concerning. Liver and kidney tests are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling better and can eat, we plan to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole twice daily, Carafate four times a day, and ranitidine twice daily. We’re also adding a daily laxative—polyethylene glycol—and increasing your senna to twice daily as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already take docusate and bisacodyl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping those too. With your history of constipation from pain meds, we want to be proactive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge orders are in. You’ll go home with all your usual meds, plus the new stomach and bowel medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should follow up with my bariatric doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your primary care provider. They’ll monitor your blood pressure, labs, and make sure the gastritis stays under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Keep taking the meds as prescribed, eat small meals, and call if the pain returns or you feel dizzy again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Pain is mild, and I’ve eaten a few snacks without nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood pressure is stable now, and you’re walking fine. We’ll get the discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. You’re being discharged with a diagnosis of gastritis, managed by resuming your previous stomach medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the bariatric team reviewed your case and agreed—no surgical issues. This was medical, and it’s responding well to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for four days now. It's in my left upper side, near the ribs, and it wraps around to my back a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it feels better after I eat. But I’ve also been feeling nauseous, especially right after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any vomiting, fever, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting or fever. I did have some loose stools the past couple days, but no blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve checked your labs and a chest X-ray to look for any serious issues. Everything looks stable—no signs of infection or free air in the abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Free air? That sounds scary. What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It would suggest a hole in the stomach or intestine, but you don’t have that. Your X-ray was clear, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked blood work—CBC, electrolytes, liver tests—and everything is normal. No signs of inflammation or organ issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—gastric bypass and reversal, multiple ulcers—it’s likely related to chronic changes in your digestive tract. The pain improving with food suggests it might be ulcer-related or visceral sensitivity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped my stomach meds a few weeks ago. Could that be why it came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very possible. Last time you were here, your pain improved when you restarted pantoprazole, sucralfate, and ranitidine. We’re going to restart those today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them. But the pain is pretty bad right now. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you morphine in the ER, and we’ll continue with acetaminophen on a schedule. We’re trying to avoid heavy narcotics since your last admission showed improvement with non-narcotic pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But if it gets bad, can I still get help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Let the nurse know, and we’ll adjust as needed. We also started a bowel regimen to keep things moving—constipation can make pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still tender, but not as sharp. The nausea is less too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’re keeping you on the stomach meds and scheduled acetaminophen. Any bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one this morning. Still a bit loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool for C. diff, and it came back negative. So it’s not an infection. We’ll give you loperamide to help control the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Also, I’ve been having double vision off and on. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned that before. Your neurology workup, including an EMG, was negative for myasthenia gravis. Since pyridostigmine can worsen GI symptoms, we’re stopping it as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. My neurologist said I could taper it. I just wasn’t sure if I should stop completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discontinuing it now. If the double vision worsens, let us know, but it’s likely part of your chronic symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs this morning are stable. White count is a bit low but not concerning. Pain still improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I’m still tender when pressed, but it doesn’t hurt on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The bariatric surgery team reviewed your case and agreed there’s no surgical issue. They recommend following up with chronic pain management for your long-term abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chronic pain? So this might not ever fully go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not that it won’t improve, but given your multiple surgeries, you may have visceral hyperalgesia—where the nerves in your gut are extra sensitive. The pain team can help manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just want to avoid ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Staying on your stomach meds, managing bowel habits, and avoiding NSAIDs will help prevent flare-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’d like to discharge you today. You’re eating, pain is controlled, and no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your stomach meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, sucralfate. Take loperamide if diarrhea returns. Stay on your bowel regimen and acetaminophen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain specialist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get a referral to the chronic pain service. They’ll help with long-term strategies. Call your PCP if symptoms worsen or don’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Your husband can come pick you up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check. Any new symptoms? Pain, nausea, dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all good. Still a little tired, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vitals are stable. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You came in with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve had loose stools, like six times a day, even though I was taking Imodium. Then I tried eating a little boiled rice and threw up twice. After that, the pain started—right here in the upper middle part of my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is epigastric—above the belly button—and it’s non-radiating. Any fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or breathing issues. Just the pain, nausea, and diarrhea. It feels kind of like the ulcer pain I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had a lot of similar episodes, and we know your history includes gastric bypass and reversal. We did a CT scan today to check things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show? Is there an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No ulcer on imaging. But the scan did show something called a gastro-gastric fistula—basically, a small connection between parts of your stomach that shouldn’t be connected. But the bariatric surgery team reviewed it and said it’s not causing an acute problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s not why I’m hurting now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The pain might be from missing your regular stomach meds. We’ve restarted your pantoprazole, sucralfate, and ranitidine. We also gave you some IV fluids and ondansetron for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did skip a few doses at home because I felt so sick. But I’m worried—could this be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable—no infection signs, no kidney or liver issues, lipase is normal. No obstruction. So no surgical emergency. We’re watching you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. But the diarrhea is still scary. Is it just from the stomach issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a stool test. If it comes back positive for C. diff, that could explain the diarrhea. It’s a bacterial infection that can happen after antibiotic use or in people with complex GI histories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Treated with Flagyl. Could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll know more tomorrow. For now, we’re holding your loperamide—Imodium—until we rule out or treat C. diff, because it can make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back: you do have C. diff. That’s likely contributing to the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we’re catching it early. We’re starting you on oral vancomycin—125 mg four times a day—for 10 days. That’s the best treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the pain? It’s still there, though a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we think the pain is from chronic issues—possibly visceral hyperalgesia, which means your nerves are extra sensitive after all the surgeries. We’ve been giving IV morphine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to rely on narcotics. Last time, I was discharged without them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re trying to avoid long-term use. But for now, we’ll use oxycodone by mouth as needed for breakthrough pain, while we treat the C. diff and get your regular meds back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain clinic appointment? I had a nerve block before, but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. The chronic pain team will see you again soon. They might suggest other options—like biofeedback or acupuncture—as part of a long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m open to that. I just want to feel more in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. How’s the pain today? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is about a 5 now, down from 8. I had a small bowl of applesauce and kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep advancing your diet slowly. Diarrhea still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but less frequent—maybe three times today. Is the vancomycin helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely starting to. It usually takes a few days. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look good. White count is normal, kidney and liver tests are stable. Pain improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about a 3-4. I had toast and tea yesterday and no issues. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep this up, probably in a day or two. We want to make sure the diarrhea is improving and you’re comfortable on oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
