conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was low-normal, around 70. We’re giving you IV fluids with dextrose to help. That should resolve the shakiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizure meds? I can’t swallow pills right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched Keppra to IV for now. Once you can keep food down, we’ll switch back to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been on oxycodone, but it didn’t help the pain at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re actually going to stop the narcotics. They can slow gut motility and worsen nausea. We’ll manage pain with Tylenol and tramadol, which are safer for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about eating? I’m really hungry but scared to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips of water. If that stays down, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow. The key is small, frequent meals—this helps reduce bile reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I kept down some apple juice last night. The nausea is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to try broth and crackers today. Also, your blood pressure was a bit low last night, but it improved with fluids. We’ve stopped the IV morphine, which was contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on propranolol for anxiety. Is that okay to restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve resumed it. Your BP is stable now. We’re also adding Carafate—a coating agent that protects your stomach while it heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need an endoscopy? I feel like we keep guessing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I spoke with GI. They don’t think an EGD is needed right now. Even if we saw inflammation, we’d treat it the same—stronger acid suppression and diet changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I just want to know what’s going on. I’ve been in and out of the hospital for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your pain has a real physical cause—bile gastritis—but there’s also a chronic component. We considered a medication like amitriptyline to help, but with your other meds, it could affect your heart rhythm, so we’re holding off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the PPI twice daily, take Carafate, eat small meals, and follow up with your gastroenterologist. You already have an outpatient EGD scheduled—that’s the right next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been eating soft foods and walking in the hall. Pain still present?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s back to my usual level—still uncomfortable, but not the sharp pain from when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s improvement. We’ll keep advancing your diet. Your labs are stable, and your blood sugar is normal now that you’re eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We want to make sure you can keep food down and manage pain with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. We’ve spoken with your GI doctor again. They agree you’re ready to go home. Pain is stable, you’re eating well, and no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad, but I’m still frustrated. We haven’t ‘fixed’ the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But we’ve addressed the acute flare—bile gastritis from stopping your meds. The chronic pain is complex, and surgery isn’t likely to help, based on your anatomy and past procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been seeing another surgeon for a second opinion about scar tissue removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But both surgery and GI teams agree that scar tissue isn’t the main issue. The focus should be on medical management and your upcoming EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take pantoprazole twice daily, Carafate four times a day, and tramadol as needed. Eat small, frequent meals. Avoid large portions—they trigger bile reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your usual medications—antidepressants, Keppra, statin, vitamins. We’ve updated your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your husband is here, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m ready, but I’ll admit I’m nervous about the pain coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, but you now know the triggers—stopping meds, large meals. If nausea or vomiting returns, call your doctor or come back. Otherwise, keep your GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the kidney finding from the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild hydronephrosis, likely from reflux. It’s not causing symptoms or blockage. Mention it to your primary doctor, but no urgent action needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate the time you’ve taken to explain everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed. Otherwise, best wishes for steady improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I be worried about the C. diff coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risk is lower now that you’re eating and off antibiotics. But if you develop diarrhea again, get tested right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood sugar—should I check it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you feel shaky or weak. It’s likely related to not eating, not true hypoglycemia. Eating regularly should prevent it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much more confident going home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more check-in before discharge. Any new pain, nausea, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still doing well. Ate breakfast and a snack. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, just to confirm—I take Carafate on an empty stomach, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one hour before or two hours after meals. Pantoprazole can be with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ve written it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you had a seizure this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my husband said I had one. I don’t remember anything after waking up. I didn’t bite my tongue or lose control, he said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with certain types of seizures. We’re also seeing signs of infection—your white blood cell count is high, and you had a fever and low blood pressure in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I don’t feel feverish now. Could that have caused the seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Infections can lower the seizure threshold, especially with high inflammation. But your neurologist will help us sort that out. We’re starting antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on Keppra for a while. I take it every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that up and may adjust the dose depending on what Neurology recommends. We also saw pneumonia on your chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? I haven’t had a cough or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it can be silent, especially with other health issues. We’re treating it with IV antibiotics—Zosyn and vancomycin—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach? I’ve been having pain when I eat too much. I vomit, but it’s not green or bloody.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan didn’t show any blockage or new surgical issues. You’re post-gastric bypass and reversal, so your anatomy is complex. That can cause these symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve had this for years. But I’m worried about getting enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted Nutrition. Given your history of hypoglycemia, we’re keeping you on D5W fluids for now to keep your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I’ve had bad lows before, even with the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that closely. One blood culture grew a common skin bacteria—coagulase-negative staph. It might be from your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should we remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discussing that with Infectious Disease. If it’s the source, we’ll remove it and continue antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your white count is coming down—from 21 to 11.5. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit more alert today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case. They recommend increasing Keppra to 1000 mg twice a day to better prevent seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I haven’t had any side effects before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common adjustment. We’ll monitor for drowsiness or dizziness, but most people tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ID team recommends removing your PICC line. It’s likely the source of the bacteria. We’ll switch to IV antibiotics through a regular IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my nutrition? I’ve been on D5W through the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you D5 with thiamine and folate through the new IV. Nutrition is also helping plan your next diet step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to eat. Last time I tried new foods, I had terrible pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re starting slow—a diabetic carb-consistent diet with six small meals. High fat, high protein, low glycemic index to avoid blood sugar swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? I need examples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Grilled chicken, avocado, eggs, cheese, nuts. Avoid sugary or starchy foods. We’ll add Glucerna shakes between meals for calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can try that. But if it hurts, can I take Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for breakthrough pain. But we’ll time it after meals to help you eat without fear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures today are negative. That’s great—means the infection is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC tip didn’t grow anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No growth. So it’s likely the initial positive was from contamination or early infection that’s now resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start eating today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with a small portion. We’ll watch for pain or nausea. Nutrition will check in after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I tried the chicken and avocado. It hurt a lot at first, but I got through half.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you had pain. We’ll give you Dilaudid as needed. The goal is to slowly retrain your stomach to tolerate food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating. I just want to eat normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But with your history, we have to be careful. We’re aiming for 1500 calories a day. Glucerna will help until you can eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures are negative. Your white count is now normal. You’re no longer septic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll switch to oral vancomycin for a few more days and stop the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I heard you did an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to check for infection on the valves. It was clean—just mild mitral regurgitation, which is common and not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two days of tolerated meals and Glucerna. No hypoglycemia. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have pain, but less. I’m drinking the shake after each meal like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if I have another seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a higher dose of Keppra now. Keep taking it. And your husband will get a nasal naloxone spray in case of oversedation from pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes me feel safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll follow up with Neurology and Endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For the seizures and blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And Nutrition will help adjust your diet at home. You need to keep eating small, frequent meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue Dilaudid as needed. But we’re also giving you senna and Colace to prevent constipation from the opioid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated before. I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a long week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has. But you’ve made real progress—no infection, better eating, and seizure meds adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last thing—we need you to get fasting insulin and C-peptide levels after discharge. It’s to check your hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do it. My husband will help me remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking your new diet seriously. It’s key to avoiding lows and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send all instructions to your husband too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with your outpatient team. You’re in good hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—take your meds as prescribed, especially Keppra. No skipping doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of new abdominal pain that’s spreading to your back. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few days ago. The usual epigastric pain I have suddenly started wrapping around to the right side and back. It’s sharper and different from my normal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers, chills, or vomiting with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. I’ve been vomiting small amounts, same as usual. But standing up makes me feel like the room is spinning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from low blood pressure or dehydration. We’ll check your vitals and get some fluids going. You mentioned your J tube—where is it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was in my abdominal wall, but the ER team said it wasn’t in the right place and took it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. The CT scan confirmed it was malpositioned—ended up in the soft tissue of your abdominal wall, not in the stomach. No infection or fluid collection, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I’ve been feeling worse? But the pain didn’t go away after removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tube wasn’t causing an infection, but its position might have been irritating. The pain continuing suggests something else is going on, or it’s part of your chronic issue flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many surgeries—gastric bypass, reversal, tubes placed and removed. I just want to know what’s causing this new pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your history. The CT and ultrasound didn’t show gallstones, pancreatitis, or obstruction. Your liver enzymes are slightly elevated but not concerning. Lactate was high when you arrived but is improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no clear cause? What about my nutrition? I’ve been struggling to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big concern. You’ve been relying on the J tube, which isn’t an option now. Eating by mouth causes pain and vomiting due to gastroparesis. The nutrition team will talk to you about balancing intake without triggering symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? I’ve been feeling shaky sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your glucose every six hours. You had one reading of 70, which is borderline low. We’re giving you dextrose in your IV fluids to keep it stable. It’s likely from not taking in enough calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about pain control? Morphine in the ER made me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to oral oxycodone, lower dose, as needed. It may help with less nausea. We’ll start low and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I don’t want to depend on narcotics, but I need some relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll aim to use the lowest effective dose and work on a long-term plan with your surgeon. Speaking of, your primary surgeon is at another center, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Evans at Mercy General. I’ve been followed there for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your complex history, we think it’s best to transfer you there. They know your case well and can discuss options like a gastric pacemaker or other interventions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be good. I trust Dr. Evans. But what about now? I still hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain with oxycodone as needed, continue IV fluids, and monitor your glucose. The nutritionist will come by to go over dietary strategies that might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team met with you. Any questions from that discussion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said small, frequent meals with liquid supplements might help, but I’m scared it’ll make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally valid. We’ll start very slowly, maybe with sips or a few spoonfuls, and see how you do. The goal isn’t to overload but to find a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vitamin levels? I remember being low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your outpatient labs showed vitamin D deficiency. We’re starting you on 50,000 units once a week. Iron is also low—we’ll discuss IV iron later as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to know. I’ve been tired—maybe that’s why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the oxycodone helps a little. I tried a few sips of protein shake—no vomiting yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your blood pressure was a bit low this morning—92/58—but improved with fluids. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dizzy when I stand. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely due to low intake and blood pressure. As we get your nutrition up, that should improve. We’ll keep you on IV fluids until you can take more by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizure meds? I took them this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levetiracetam is continued twice daily. No changes there. Your last seizure was months ago, so we’re keeping it consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve got your transfer approved to Mercy General. They’ll admit you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Will they consider another feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s risky given your history of misplacement and surgeries. They may discuss IV nutrition or other options, but it’s something to talk through with your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to keep ending up in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all want that. The goal is to get you stabilized and work on a long-term plan. They may also evaluate the gastric pacer for gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was mentioned before. I’m willing to try anything that might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day—we’re transferring you to Mercy General. Your condition is stable: pain controlled, vitals normal, no fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. What meds am I going with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your home meds continue: levetiracetam, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, metoclopramide, and the others. Plus, oxycodone for breakthrough pain and weekly vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should keep trying small meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, slowly. And keep monitoring your blood sugar if you can. The team at Mercy will guide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and I hope the next visit is for a follow-up, not another admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will be here soon. Your husband is on the way to meet you there, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll be waiting. I feel better knowing I’m going to a team that knows my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes a big difference. They’ll coordinate with pain management, nutrition, and surgery. We’ll send all your records over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wound site? The G-tube area is still draining a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s clean, with serosanguinous drainage—normal after removal. Keep it covered, and the team will check it daily. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll include wound care instructions in your transfer summary. You’re doing well—just keep up the slow progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and I’ll let the team at Mercy know you’re on your way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what happened before you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I stood up from my chair and suddenly the room started spinning. The next thing I remember, I was on the floor. My son saw it—he said I was out for about five minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you have any jerking movements, bite your tongue, or lose bladder control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. I just blacked out. I’ve had seizures before, but this didn’t feel like one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. You also mentioned nausea, abdominal pain, and slurred speech this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain in my stomach has been worse since my hiatal hernia surgery three weeks ago. I can’t keep much down—just a little water and a protein shake a day. And this morning, my words were a bit slurred.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s concerning. We’ve given you fluids in the ER and checked your vitals. Your blood pressure dropped when you stood up, which suggests you may have fainted due to low blood volume from not eating or drinking enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. Your CT scan of the head and neck showed no stroke or bleeding, and your MRI was normal. Neurology reviewed it and agrees—no signs of a seizure this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why am I so dizzy and weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from dehydration and poor nutrition. You’ve lost weight, and your labs show you’re not getting enough calories. We’re going to keep you on IV fluids and monitor your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been struggling to eat since the surgery. Everything makes me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your history of gastric bypass and recent reversal makes digestion difficult. We’re consulting GI to help figure out the best way to support your nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and your blood pressure is improving with fluids. But you’re still having epigastric pain and nausea. We’re going to try a stronger acid blocker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on omeprazole. Why switch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting pantoprazole twice a day because your endoscopy showed irritation and a narrowing at the stomach junction. This medication will help reduce acid and let it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already had one. Two days ago, during the endoscopy, they dilated the narrowed area with a balloon. It went well, but you’re still not tolerating food, so we need to think about longer-term nutrition support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering placing a feeding tube that goes past your stomach into the small intestine. That way, we can give you nutrition without relying on your stomach emptying properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like a feeding tube in my nose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a Dobhoff tube. It’s thin and goes through your nose, down into your intestine. It’s temporary—we’ll see how you do and plan next steps with your bariatric surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI came back normal, which is great news. No signs of a stroke or seizure focus. But neurology still wants to rule out any subtle brainstem issues, so they recommend an ENT visit and autonomic testing after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Autonomic testing? What’s that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It checks how your body regulates things like blood pressure and heart rate when you stand up. Since you fainted, we want to see if there’s an issue with that system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been discussing your case with GI and nutrition. Because you’re still not eating and your weight is low, we think it’s best to go ahead with the Dobhoff tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When would that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow. It’s done during another endoscopy, and they’ll place it past your stomach so food bypasses the slow area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get nutrition through it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start tube feeds slowly and monitor you. The goal is to improve your strength and prevent more fainting episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube was placed successfully. It’s now in your small intestine, and we’ve started a slow rate of tube feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel nasal discomfort, but it usually gets better. We’ve secured it so it doesn’t pull. Let us know if it becomes painful or dislodges.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff, so we can rule that out as a cause of your nausea and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Your dizziness has improved, and your blood pressure is stable. We’ve increased your tube feeds, and you’re getting more calories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit stronger. But will I ever eat normally again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. That’s something to discuss with your bariatric surgeon. For now, the tube is helping your body heal and get the nutrition it needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your albumin and electrolytes are normal, and your kidney function is good. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad I’m not passing out anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You’ll go home with the feeding tube and continue the feeds. A nurse will help you set it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to do this myself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but with support. A home health nurse will train you and your family. You’ll also follow up with GI, your PCP, and your bariatric surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual medications—Keppra for seizures, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and the new pantoprazole. We’ve added sucralfate to protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on full tube feeds for 24 hours with no issues. Your abdominal pain is milder, and you’re walking without dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m ready to go home, but I’m nervous about managing the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. The home care team will visit you tomorrow to train you. They’ll show you how to give the feeds, clean the tube, and troubleshoot problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The home health nurse met with you and reviewed everything. Any questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting or the tube stops working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your GI doctor or come back if you have severe pain, fever, or the tube comes out. For minor issues, the nurse gave you a contact number.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see GI in one week, your PCP in two weeks, and your bariatric surgeon soon after. We’ve also referred you for autonomic testing and ENT to check the dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And neurology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They want to consider an EMU admission later to better understand your seizure history, but that’s not urgent now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had another good night. Your vitals are stable, and you’re tolerating the tube well. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Thank you for helping me get stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. Just keep up with the feeds, take your meds, and keep those follow-ups. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You’ll go home with instructions, prescriptions, and your tube supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to follow up with your bariatric surgeon about long-term feeding options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep using the lidocaine patch for your knee pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And don’t forget your vitamin D once a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.
